licoes.t: Awakening from the Matrix: The Map
p: like waking up from the matrix
awakening from the matrix the map
licoes.r: Waking up from the Matrix is realizing the programs running in your mind that you didn't choose. Expanding consciousness is gaining space to choose. This path brings together three sources, each with its own stamp: the research of psychology and neuroscience, the wisdom of tradition, and what no one yet knows. Say wake-up lessons to see the full list.
licoes.a: The map has four gates. First, look at the program: conditioning, advertising, repetition and biases, all studied in the lab. Second, to see who sees: the attention, the observer self and the reality-predicting brain. Third, training: meditation, lucid dreaming, state of flow and neuroplasticity. Fourth, don't get lost along the way: separate tradition from fact and recognize spiritual deviance. Practice: pick a gate

licoes.r: Science doesn't measure the expansion of consciousness the way mystics talk about it, but it measures states of consciousness. In 1969, psychologist Charles Tart published Altered States of Consciousness, and today sleep, dreaming, meditation, hypnosis, and the effect of substances are studied with electroencephalogram and MRI.
licoes.a: In 2013, Italian and American researchers created a brain complexity index that accurately separates people who are awake, asleep, anesthetized, or in a coma. In 2017, a study showed that psychedelics increase the diversity of brain signals above normal wakefulness. It doesn't prove that the person has become wiser; it shows that the brain has become more variable, and what that means is still a hypothesis. Expansion

licoes.r: In Plato's cave, prisoners saw shadows projected by others and thought they were reality. Today, the wall is the screen, and the shadow picker is an algorithm. In 2011, activist Eli Pariser called this a filter bubble: each person is given a custom-made world to capture their attention.
licoes.a: The whole truth: studies published in 2023 in the journals Science and Nature, using data from Facebook and Instagram, showed that the separation exists, but that changing the algorithm for a few months hardly changed people's political views. p: how do we know if we re living in a simulation
como saber se vivemos numa simulacao
licoes.r: Nick Bostrom's 2003 argument does not say that we live in a simulation. It says that at least one of three things is true: almost all civilizations go extinct before they can simulate worlds; or those that do don't; or we almost certainly live in a simulation. No one knows which of the three is the real one.
licoes.a: In 2012, physicists Silas Beane, Zohreh Davoudi and Martin Savage proposed looking for signs of a simulation grid in very high-energy cosmic rays; nothing has been found to date. Critics, such as physicist Sabine Hossenfelder, say that without a possible test, the idea is closer to philosophy than science. Bostrom himself does not claim that we live in a simulation. licoes.t: The Brain as a Filter for Reality
p: the brain as a filter for reality
licoes.r: You don't see the world directly: your brain assembles an image of it. That's been proven. Each eye has a blind spot, no light receptor, and you can't see the hole because your brain fills it. In 2015, a photo of a dress divided the world into blue and black and white and gold: the same image, different brains.
licoes.a: The strongest hypothesis today, called predictive processing, says that the brain works the opposite of what we think: it predicts what you're going to perceive and uses your senses to correct the guess. Hermann von Helmholtz already spoke of unconscious inference in the 19th century. Neuroscientist Anil Seth, in his 2021 book Being You, sums it up: perception is a reality-controlled hallucination. licoes.t: Default mode network: the inner chatterbox
p: default mode network the inner chatterbox
licoes.r: In 2001, neuroscientist Marcus Raichle described a brain network that becomes most active when you're not focused on anything: the default mode network. It's connected to thinking about yourself, ruminating on the past and imagining the future. It's largely the voice that talks nonstop inside your head.
licoes.a: In 2010, a Harvard study of more than 2,000 people showed that the mind wanders for almost half of the time you're awake, and that a wandering mind is a less happy mind. In 2011, Judson Brewer showed that experienced meditators have less activity in this network when meditating, and in 2012, Robin Carhart-Harris saw something similar to psilocybin. Careful, that doesn't make psychedelics a shortcut to enlightenment.

p: a lie repeated a thousand times
licoes.r: In 1977, psychologists Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino showed that a repeated sentence seems more true even when it is false. It's the effect of illusory truth: the brain confuses what's familiar with what's real.
licoes.a: In 2015, psychologist Lisa Fazio showed that not even knowing the right answer completely protects: repetition deceives even those who know. That's why slogans, jingles, pulpit sticks and message boards work. Honest curiosity: the phrase a lie repeated a thousand times becomes truth is always attributed to Goebbels, but no one has found this phrase in his writings. The quote itself is an example of the effect. Practi

licoes.t: Cognitive bias: the code of the Matrix.
p: cognitive bias the code of the matrix
licoes.r: If the Matrix had a source code, it would be cognitive biases, automatic shortcuts from the mind. In 1974, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described several of them, and Kahneman won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002. In his 2011 book Fast and Slow, he separates System 1, fast and automatic, from System 2, slow and reflexive.
licoes.a: Examples. Anchoring: In one experiment, a roulette wheel that stopped at 10 or 65 changed people's guess about the percentage of African countries in the UN. Availability: We find more common what we remember easily, like a plane crash seen on TV. Confirmation: We only look for what confirms what we already believe. No one gets rid of biases; you can recognize them and slow them down. Practice: Before making an impor

licoes.t: Attention: the power of the observer
p: attention the power of the observer
licoes.r: In 1999, psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked volunteers to count ball passes in a video. About half didn't see a person in a gorilla costume walk through the scene. It's inattentional blindness: what you don't respond to, to you, doesn't exist.
licoes.a: The psychologist William James wrote, in 1890, "My experience is what I agree to pay attention to". So attention is the most contested resource in the world: whoever controls your attention controls the reality you live in. Contemplative traditions have taught this for millennia. The observer of quantum physics is something else: it's physical measurement, not the human mind. Practice: For ten minutes today, give you

licoes.t: States of consciousness: Gurdjieff and Wilber
p: states of consciousness gurdjieff and wilber
licoes.r: For George Gurdjieff, a master born in Armenia in the late nineteenth century, the average human being lives sleeping with his eyes open. According to the account of the disciple Piotr Ouspensky, in the book Fragments of an Unknown Teaching, he spoke of four states: sleep, ordinary wakefulness, which he called waking sleep, self-consciousness, and objective consciousness.
licoes.a: The path, for him, was self-remembering: being present to oneself while acting. In the late 20th century, philosopher Ken Wilber put together the integral theory, a map that links stages of developmental psychology with states described by contemplative traditions. They're maps of tradition and philosophy, useful for reflection, but no one's proven that consciousness goes up those stairs. Practice: set three alarms t

licoes.r: Psychiatrist David Hawkins, in his 1995 book Power versus Strength, created a scale of consciousness from one to a thousand: from shame, to twenty, to courage, to two hundred, and love, to five hundred, to enlightenment, to seven hundred to a thousand. The numbers were obtained by muscle testing, so-called applied kinesiology, and that's where the problem lies.
licoes.a: In controlled trials, in which neither the tester nor the test subject knows the correct answer, the muscle test did not fare better than chance, as in a 1988 study published in the Journal of the American Dietetic Association. So Hawkins' calibrations of people, books and countries have no measurable value. As a reflection map, the idea that courage comes before love can inspire; as a science, it doesn't hold up. Pr

licoes.r: There's something in you that understands thoughts without being any of them. The Indian tradition of Vedanta calls it sakshi, the witness. Modern psychology uses the same idea: acceptance and commitment therapy, by Steven Hayes, talks about the self as context, and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy talks about decentralization.
licoes.a: Decentralization is seeing a thought as an event in the mind, not as a fact about the world. Clinical research shows that such therapy reduces relapses in those who have had multiple bouts of depression. Ramana Maharshi, the 20th-century Indian sage, taught one question: Who am I? Not to answer with words, but to direct attention to the questioner. Practice: When a heavy thought comes, put it in front: I'm having tha

licoes.t: Lucid dreaming: training to wake up
p: a lucid dream and waking up
lucid dreaming training to wake up
licoes.r: In 2021, teams from four countries, the United States, France, Germany and the Netherlands, talked to people during lucid dreaming: they asked simple questions and calculations, and the dreamers answered with eye movements, without waking up. The study appeared in the journal Current Biology. Waking up inside the dream is real and can be trained.
licoes.a: The most widely studied technique is Stephen LaBerge's MILD: when you wake up in the morning, you repeat the intention, the next time you dream, I'll realize I'm dreaming, and imagine the dream coming back to you lucid. In 2017, an Australian study by Denholm Aspy combined this with reality tests and waking up in the middle of the night; among those who went back to sleep quickly, almost half of the attempts were suc

licoes.r: Psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi has studied for decades the moments when people feel most alive. In 1990, in his book Flow, he described the state of flow: total attention, time seems to disappear, the voice being criticized becomes silent, and the action flows almost by itself.
licoes.a: Flow comes when the challenge is slightly greater than the skill, with clear goals and immediate feedback. Too much challenge creates anxiety; too little, boredom. Athletes, musicians, craftsmen and surgeons describe the same state. It's one of the healthiest doors to egoless consciousness, because it's born of presence, not flight. licoes.r: In 1979, Jon Kabat-Zinn created at the University of Massachusetts an eight-week stress reduction program based on mindfulness. In 2014, a major review in JAMA Internal Medicine of 47 studies found moderate evidence of improvement in anxiety, depression, and pain.
licoes.a: The whole truth includes boundaries. The same review did not find meditation superior to other active treatments, such as exercise or therapy. In 2018, a group of researchers published the article Mind the Hype, warning of hype in the media. And in 2017, a study by Jared Lindahl and Willoughby Britton documented difficult experiences in meditators, such as fear and feelings of unreality. Meditation is powerful; it is

licoes.r: Kundalini, in the tradition of tantra and hatha yoga, is an energy described as a sleeping snake at the base of the spine, rising through the chakras, subtle centers, to the top of the head. It's a teaching of tradition, centuries of practice, not a fact of anatomy.
licoes.a: Facts: The seven-chakra system known in the West comes mostly from a 1577 Indian text translated in 1919 by John Woodroffe in The Power of the Serpent. Older texts give different numbers of chakras, and the colors of the rainbow are a 20th-century Western creation. No tests found chakras on the body. Serious teachers warn that intense energy practices without guidance can lead to crises. Practice: Use your chakras as

p: the whole and mind and science
o todo e mente e a ciencia
licoes.r: The Caibalion, 1908, teaches that the Whole is Mind. Neuroscience shows something more modest but real: your mind depends on your brain, because anesthesia, deep sleep, and injury change or erase your consciousness. At the same time, no one has yet explained why feeling exists. Both things are true at the same time.
licoes.a: In philosophy, the idea that reality is mental is called idealism. Bishop George Berkeley wrote in 1710 that to be is to be perceived. Today, some thinkers, such as Bernardo Kastrup, advocate modern idealism, others panpsychism, and most neuroscientists work with the hypothesis that consciousness arises from the brain. None of this is proven. What's proven to be more practical is that the way you interpret a fact cha

licoes.t: Signs of Spiritual Awakening and Departure
p: signs of spiritual awakening and departure
licoes.r: Signs of a true awakening, according to tradition: less reactivity, more honesty with yourself, more compassion and less need to be right. On the other hand, lists of ascension symptoms, such as ringing in the ear, headache, or tiredness as evidence of awakening, are myths: These symptoms have causes in the body and merit medical examination.
licoes.a: In 1984, psychotherapist John Welwood coined the term spiritual deviance: using spirituality to escape from wounds, anger, grief, or practical problems. Examples: saying that everything is an illusion to avoid facing a conflict, or having someone vibrate loudly to silence a pain. p: get out of the matrix in practice
how to check a news story
getting out of the matrix in practice
licoes.r: Three steps with evidence. One, media diet: In an experiment published in 2020 in American Economic Review, people who turned off Facebook for four weeks spent more time with family and friends, became a little less polarized, and reported more well-being. Two, critical thinking. Three, silence.
licoes.a: Critical thinking in practice: Stanford researchers, with Sam Wineburg, found that professional reviewers don't read a website from top to bottom; they open other tabs and look up who's behind it. This is called lateral reading. Mike Caulfield's SIFT method is summarized in four steps: stop, investigate the source, find better coverage, and trace the claim back to the source. And silence: a time a day without any sti

licoes.r: The adult brain changes with use. In 2000, neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire showed that taxi drivers in London, who line thousands of streets, have the back of the hippocampus, which is connected to spatial memory, larger than other people. In 2004, another study saw changes in the brains of people who learned to juggle in three months.
licoes.a: Psychologist Donald Hebb proposed in 1949 the rule that neuroscientist Carla Shatz summarized as follows: neurons firing together connect. Every repeated habit strengthens a path, and every abandoned path weakens it. Honesty: the word has become marketing. No ten-minute audio reprograms the brain, and the twenty-one-day story is a myth: In 2010, a study by Phillippa Lally found an average of sixty-six days for a habi

p: hebb s rule neurons firing together
licoes.r: In 1949, Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb proposed in his book The Organization of Behavior that when one neuron repeatedly helps to fire another, the bond between the two is strengthened. The popular phrase, neurons firing together connect, is a summary made later. Today, this idea is one of the cornerstones of memory science.
licoes.a: The proof came in 1973: Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo stimulated the hippocampus of rabbits with electrical bursts and saw the synapses respond more strongly for hours, sometimes days. They called it long-lasting enhancement. Eric Kandel, studying the sea slug Aplysia, showed that short memories change the strength of synapses, and that long memories require new proteins and even new connections; he won the Nobel Priz

licoes.t: Taxi Drivers and Musicians - The Brain That Trains
p: taxi drivers and musicians - the brain that trains
licoes.r: To get their licence, London taxi drivers spend three to four years memorizing about 25,000 streets. In 2011, Katherine Woollett and Eleanor Maguire followed seventy-nine learners: those who passed the test gained volume in the back of the hippocampus; those who did not and the comparison group did not. It was proof that training changes the brain, and not just that different brains choose careers.
licoes.a: But there's a price. In 2006, Maguire's team compared taxi drivers to bus drivers, who drive all day on fixed routes: Taxi drivers had the back of the hippocampus larger and the front smaller, and did worse at memorizing a new figure. The brain reallocates space, it doesn't grow for free. In musicians: In 1995, Thomas Elbert and colleagues showed that violinists and cellists have a larger area in the cortex for the f

licoes.t: Does meditation change the brain? What Is Really Known
p: does meditation change the brain what is really known
licoes.r: That meditation changes brain activity during practice is well established. Whether it changes the structure of the brain is still up for debate. In 2005, Harvard's Sara Lazar found thicker cortex in areas of attention and body perception in 20 experienced meditators compared to 15 non-meditators.
licoes.a: In 2004, Antoine Lutz and Richard Davidson recorded very strong gamma waves in Tibetan monks with tens of thousands of hours of practice, but there were only eight monks. In 2011, Britta Hölzel reported more gray matter in the hippocampus after eight weeks of the stress reduction program with sixteen people. licoes.t: Adult neurogenesis: are new neurons born?
p: adult neurogenesis are new neurons born
licoes.r: For almost a century, it has been taught that the adult brain does not gain new neurons. In mice and rats, it's now proven to win in the hippocampus. In adult humans, the question remains open, and serious laboratories have come up with conflicting answers.
licoes.a: In 1998, Peter Eriksson and Fred Gage found new neurons in the hippocampus of cancer patients who had received a cell division marker. In 2013, Jonas Frisén's team used the carbon-14 scattered in the air by nuclear tests and estimated about 700 new neurons a day in each hippocampus. In 2018, the journal Nature published Shawn Sorrells' study, which found virtually no new neurons after childhood; in the same year, Mau

licoes.t: Brain maps: Merzenich, Taub and the aftermath of a stroke
p: brain maps merzenich, taub and the aftermath of a stroke
licoes.r: In the 1980s, Michael Merzenich showed in monkeys that the map of the body inside the brain changes: when one finger stopped sending signals, its area was used by the neighboring fingers. Psychologist Edward Taub turned this idea into a treatment for stroke patients: limiting the good arm to force the weak arm to work.
licoes.a: Taub called the problem not-learned use: After a stroke, the person gives up the weak arm, and the brain shrinks its space even further. In induced restraint therapy, the healthy arm stays in a glove for a good portion of the day, and the weak arm trains for several hours a day for two weeks. In 2006, the EXCITE trial of 222 patients, published in the journal JAMA, showed greater improvement than standard treatment,

licoes.t: Critical periods - the windows of childhood
p: critical periods - the windows of childhood
licoes.r: Some brain capacities have windows in which they form much more easily. In the 1960s, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel closed the eye of a kitten for a few months, and that eye lost much of its connection to the brain. In adult cats, the same thing didn't happen. They won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1981.
licoes.a: In children, it's the logic of amblyopia, the lazy eye: treated early, with a tampon or glasses, usually has good results; treated late, the gain is usually less. With language too: those who learn a language after adolescence rarely lose their accent. In 2018, a study of about six hundred and seventy thousand people estimated that the ease of mastering the grammar of a new language drops around the age of seventeen.

licoes.t: Sleep: When the brain records the day
p: sleep when the brain records the day
licoes.r: Sleep is not shutting down: it's when the brain organizes what it's learned. In 1924, John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach showed that people forgot less of a list of syllables when they slept after studying than when they woke up. Today, that sleep helps fix memories is one of science's most repeated findings.
licoes.a: In 1994, Matthew Wilson and Bruce McNaughton saw, in mice, hippocampal neurons repeating during sleep the sequence of paths taken in the maze, much like a daydreamer. In 2002, Matthew Walker showed that people who trained a sequence of fingers on the keyboard got faster after a night's sleep, without further training. The idea that sleep washes the brain, through the so-called glymphatic system, came from studies on

licoes.t: Habits: the autopilot of the base ganglia
p: habits the autopilot of the base ganglia
licoes.r: When an action becomes a habit, the command passes from the front areas of the brain, which decide, to the basal ganglia, a set of nuclei at the back of it. Neuroscientist Ann Graybiel at MIT has seen in mice that with repetition, the neurons in the striatum start firing loudly at the beginning and end of the routine, as if they were packing everything into one block.
licoes.a: So habit dispenses with decision: one trigger fires the whole pack. In 2002, Wendy Wood and colleagues asked people to write down what they did throughout the day: About 43 percent of the actions were repeated almost every day in the same place, often while the person was thinking about something else. Two lessons have good evidence. First, habits depend on the environment; changing your home, your route, or your sch

licoes.t: The placebo effect: the real power of expectation
p: the placebo effect the real power of expectation
licoes.r: The placebo is real, but it's not magic. In 1978, Jon Levine and colleagues gave fake medicine to patients with tooth extraction pain; many felt relief, and that relief was lessened with naloxone, which blocks the body's natural morphine. The anticipation made the brain release its own painkillers.
licoes.a: In 2001, a study in the journal Science showed that Parkinson's patients released dopamine into the brain when they thought they had been given the drug. In 2010, Ted Kaptchuk of Harvard gave a placebo to 80 people with irritable bowel syndrome, openly telling them it was a placebo, and even so their symptoms improved more than in the group that got nothing; how this works is still a hypothesis. Now the limits: a 201

licoes.t: Stress and Exercise: What Shrinks and What Feeds the Hippocampus
p: stress and exercise what shrinks and what feeds the hippocampus
licoes.r: Endless stress and regular movement pull the hippocampus, the center of memory, in opposite directions. In 2011, Kirk Erickson and colleagues randomly assigned 120 older adults: those who walked three times a week for a year had a hippocampus about two percent larger; in the group that only did stretching, it shrank a little, as is common with age.
licoes.a: In the same study, the increase was accompanied by BDNF, a protein that functions as a fertilizer for neurons; in 1999, Henriette van Praag had already seen that mice that ran on the wheel produced more new neurons. On the other hand, cortisol, the stress hormone, in excess and for a long time damages neurons in the hippocampus in animals, as Robert Sapolsky's work has shown; and people with Cushing's syndrome, who p

licoes.t: Reprogramming beliefs in practice: reassessment and cognitive therapy
p: reprogramming beliefs in practice reassessment and cognitive therapy
licoes.r: Beliefs cannot be changed by decree, but they can be tested and reviewed. In the '60s, psychiatrist Aaron Beck realized that depressed patients had automatic thoughts, like I always fail, that they accepted without examining. This was the birth of cognitive behavioral therapy, now one of the most studied psychotherapies in the world.
licoes.a: The central technique is called cognitive reassessment: note the thought, look for the evidence for and against it, and assemble a fairer reading. Imaging studies, like those by Kevin Ochsner and James Gross, show that reevaluating a situation activates areas of the front of the brain and decreases the amygdala response, which is linked to fear. licoes.t: Myth: Left brain and right brain
p: myth left brain and right brain
licoes.r: Myth: There are no left-brained, logical people and right-brained, creative people. In 2013, researchers at the University of Utah analyzed scans of more than 1,000 people and found no one who used one whole side of the brain more than the other.
licoes.a: The real seed of the myth: some functions hang to one side. In the vast majority of right-handed people, language is more on the left side, as Paul Broca and Carl Wernicke pointed out in the 19th century. And Roger Sperry, studying people who had the connection between the two halves cut off to treat severe epilepsy, showed that each half processes things in a different way; he won the Nobel Prize in 1981. That's bee

licoes.t: Reprogram DNA with your mind? Epigenetics without exaggeration
p: reprogram dna with your mind epigenetics without exaggeration
licoes.r: Myth: Thoughts don't rewrite the letters of your DNA, and there are no dormant strands of DNA to activate. What's real has another name, epigenetics: chemical markers that turn genes on and off, and that change with diet, stress, smoking and age.
licoes.a: The most famous example comes from the Dutch famine winter of 1944 and 1945: a 2008 study showed that six decades later, people who were in the womb during the famine had different markings on a gene linked to growth. That's been proven. And studies of meditation and genes, like one from 2014 in which 19 experienced meditators showed a decrease in inflammation gene activity after a day of practice, are small and prel

licoes.t: Metacognition and neuroplasticity: the mind and the brain
p: awareness of one s own thinking
metacognition and neuroplasticity the mind and the brain
licoes.r: Metacognition is thinking about your own thinking: realizing what you know, what you don't know, and how your mind is working right now. Neuroplasticity is another thing: it's the brain physically changing with use, in synapses and connections. One is a function of the mind; the other is a change in the organ. And the two of them work together.
licoes.a: Think of a ship. Neuroplasticity is the hull being slowly reshaped by the journey itself; metacognition is the captain looking at the map and correcting the course. On its own, plasticity reinforces anything that repeats itself, including fear and addiction. Metacognition helps you choose what's worth repeating. licoes.t: Flavell, Nelson and Narens: knowing, watching and controlling
p: flavell, nelson and narens knowing, watching and controlling
licoes.r: In 1979, the American psychologist John Flavell, who studied children, popularized the name metacognition and separated it into two parts: knowledge about how the mind works, for example knowing that you forget names, and regulation, which is using that knowledge to plan, check, and correct. In 1990, Thomas Nelson and Louis Narens described the mechanism: a monitoring level and a controlling level.
licoes.a: In Nelson and Narens' model, there are two floors. At the bottom, the mind works: it reads, remembers, solves. Upstairs, she watches herself. Monitoring is the information that comes up: that I already know, that is difficult, that word is on the tip of my tongue. Control is the descending order: study more, change strategy, stop trying. If monitoring is wrong, control is wrong too: those who think they already know

licoes.t: Calibration: certainty, accuracy and the Dunning-Kruger effect
p: he who knows little thinks he knows much
calibration certainty, accuracy and the dunning-kruger effect
quem sabe pouco acha que sabe muito
licoes.r: Calibration is how much your certainty matches your accuracy: whoever says ninety percent sure should get it right nine times out of ten. For most people, certainty is more important than success. In 1999, Justin Kruger and David Dunning showed that participants with the lowest scores on tests of logic, grammar and humor were, on average, in the 12th percentile, but placed themselves in the 62nd.
licoes.a: Kruger and Dunning explained it this way: the same skill that is lacking to do well is needed to realize that one has done wrong. Now the honest criticism: since 2016, Edward Nuhfer and colleagues, and then Gilles Gignac and Marcin Zajenkowski, have shown that much of the famous graph appears even with randomly drawn data, by a statistical effect called mean regression, coupled with the general tendency of everyone t

licoes.r: Do you know how a zipper works? Almost everyone says yes, until I try to explain step by step. In 2002, Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil of Yale University asked people to rate how much they understood about common objects, such as zippers, drains, and locks; after they wrote down the explanation, the ratings they gave themselves plummeted.
licoes.a: The illusion is stronger for mechanisms, things with gears and causes, than for loose facts or stories. In 2013, Philip Fernbach and colleagues took this to politics: asking people to explain how a proposal would work, step by step, decreased certainty and made opinions less extreme; asking only for reasons for one's position did not have the same effect. Part of the illusion comes from something healthy: we live in

licoes.t: Measure metacognition: the meta-d line and the prefrontal cortex
p: measure metacognition the meta-d line and the prefrontal cortex
licoes.r: Metacognition can be measured. In simple tasks, the person answers and then says how much he or she trusts the answer. People with good metacognitive sensitivity trust more when they're right and less when they're wrong. In 2012, Brian Maniscalco and Hakwan Lau created a measure called the meta-d line, which separates this sensitivity from performance on the task itself.
licoes.a: In 2010, Stephen Fleming and colleagues in London showed in the journal Science that people with more precise introspection on a visual task had more gray matter in the anterior prefrontal cortex, the most forward part of the brain, which is highly developed in humans. In 2014, the same Fleming studied seven patients with lesions in this area: metacognition worsened in perceptual tasks, but not in memory tasks. The c

licoes.t: Learning to learn: the illusion of fluency and recovery practice
p: learning to learn the illusion of fluency and recovery practice
licoes.r: Re-reading and scribbling give the feeling of having learned, because the text is familiar. It's called the fluency illusion. In 2006, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke showed that students who tested themselves remembered much more after a week than those who only repeated, although those who repeated felt more confident.
licoes.a: The problem is metacognitive: we judge learning by the ease of the moment, and ease deceives. A 2013 review by John Dunlosky and colleagues evaluated ten study techniques: test practice and spaced study scored high; scribbling and rereading scored low. Another useful finding: judgments about whether you've learned are much more accurate when they're made a while later, rather than right after you've studied, as Thoma

licoes.t: Metacognitive therapy: the beliefs behind worry
p: metacognitive therapy the beliefs behind worry
licoes.r: The British psychologist Adrian Wells proposed in the 1990s that the problem with anxiety and depression is not just what we think, but what we believe about thinking. Beliefs like worrying protects me, or I can't control my thoughts, keep my mind stuck in worry and rumination. He created metacognitive therapy to mess with those beliefs.
licoes.a: Wells calls this pattern cognitive-attentional syndrome: worrying, ruminating, watching for threats and trying to suppress thoughts. Positive beliefs say that worry helps; negative beliefs say that it is dangerous and uncontrollable. The two together form the trap. Instead of discussing the content of each fear, therapy teaches you to let go and postpone worrying for a set time. A 2018 meta-analysis by Nicoline Norma

licoes.t: Decentralization: Thought is an event, not a fact
p: decentralization thought is an event, not a fact
licoes.r: Decentralization is taking a step back and seeing a thought as a mind event, and not as the truth about yourself or about the world. In 2002, John Teasdale and colleagues showed that this ability, which they called metacognitive awareness, grew with mindfulness-based cognitive therapy and was linked to fewer relapses of depression.
licoes.a: In the 2000 trial, Teasdale, Zindel Segal, and Mark Williams followed 145 people recovering from depression. Among those who had already had three or more seizures, the relapse dropped from sixty-six to thirty-seven percent with the program. In 2016, Willem Kuyken gathered the individual data of one thousand two hundred and fifty-eight patients from nine trials: the risk of relapse in just over a year was about thirt

licoes.t: Cognitive effusion: letting go of the hook of words
p: cognitive effusion letting go of the hook of words
licoes.r: In acceptance and commitment therapy, created by Steven Hayes, fusion is when you and thought see one thing only: I'm a failure ceases to be a phrase and becomes reality. Diffusion is perceiving words as words, sounds and images in the mind, without obeying them and without fighting with them.
licoes.a: An old technique shows the effect: in 1916, psychologist Edward Titchener noticed that repeating a word too many times, like milk, milk, milk, causes it to lose meaning for a moment. In 2004, Akihiko Masuda and colleagues asked people to repeat out loud, quickly, a word linked to a negative thought about themselves; the discomfort and credibility of the thought dropped more than with distraction or with attempts to c

licoes.t: System 2 to the rescue? The limits of debiasing
p: system 2 to the rescue the limits of debiasing
licoes.r: Knowing that biases exist is not enough to escape them. In 2012, Richard West, Russell Meserve and Keith Stanovich showed that people with higher cognitive ability did not have a blind spot of minor bias: they continued to see biases in others more than in themselves, and sometimes even more.
licoes.a: Still, some training works a little. Consider the opposite technique, tested by Charles Lord, Mark Lepper and Elizabeth Preston in 1984, reduced confirmation bias better than just asking people to be impartial. In 2019, Anne-Laure Sellier, Irene Scopelliti, and Carey Morewedge gave a training set against confirmation bias to two hundred and ninety graduate students; then, in a business case without any warning, inspi

licoes.r: Intellectual humility is recognizing that your beliefs may be wrong. In 2017, Mark Leary and colleagues at Duke University showed that people with higher intellectual humility paid more attention to the strength of their arguments, judged others less for their religious views, and didn't see a politician changing his mind as a weakness.
licoes.a: Psychologist Jonathan Baron calls actively open thinking the habit of seeking evidence against what you think and weighing that evidence fairly. In the Good Judgment Project forecasting tournament, the best forecasters, called super forecasters, scored higher on this way of thinking. Intellectual humility is not to be without convictions, nor to think that every opinion is worth the same: it is to hold convictions wi

licoes.r: No one can check everything by himself; we live by trusting others. In 2010, anthropologist Dan Sperber and colleagues called epistemic surveillance the set of defenses we use to avoid being deceived: we evaluate who's speaking, whether they're competent, whether they're interested, and whether what they're saying matches what we already know.
licoes.a: It shows up early: Three- and four-year-olds already prefer to learn from the one who got it right before the one who got it wrong. Cognitive scientist Hugo Mercier, in his 2020 book Not Born Yesterday, argues that we are less gullible than we think; the greatest danger is when surveillance is intentionally turned off, such as when we are taught that asking is rebellion or lack of faith. Three questions are helpful b

licoes.t: Lucid dreaming and metacognition: the same light on?
p: lucid dreaming and metacognition the same light on
licoes.r: Lucid dreaming is knowing you're dreaming without waking up, and that's an act of metacognition: the mind perceives its own state. In 2015, Elisa Filevich and colleagues at the Max Planck Institute in Berlin found that people who have lucid dreams frequently have more gray matter in the frontal cortex, a region that also activates when we monitor our own waking thoughts.
licoes.a: In the same study, this region became more active in lucid dreamers during a task of monitoring one's thoughts. It was already known that in ordinary dreams, the frontal lobes of the brain become less active, which helps explain why we accept absurdities without being surprised. licoes.t: Witness and meta-consciousness: tradition and science
p: witness and meta-consciousness tradition and science
licoes.r: Contemplative traditions speak of a witness: the consciousness that sees thoughts without being swept away by them. In the Vedanta, it's called sakshi. Science can't confirm an eternal witness, but it studies something nearby and measurable: meta-consciousness, the moment you realize where your attention has gone.
licoes.a: Psychologist Jonathan Schooler has shown that the mind wanders in two ways: when you know you're distracted, and when it wanders without realizing it, like reading a whole page without remembering anything. It's the second way, without meta-consciousness, that gets you the most wrong. In 2015, Cortland Dahl, Antoine Lutz, and Richard Davidson proposed dividing meditations into three families: those of attention, thos

licoes.t: Advanced protocol: metacognitive diary and the mirror question
p: advanced protocol metacognitive diary and the mirror question
licoes.r: This is a 10-minute daily workout that combines what the previous lessons showed. At night, write down a time during the day when you felt certain, felt strongly, or decided something. Then ask the mirror question: If I believed otherwise, what evidence would I be looking for, and what would I be seeing now?
licoes.a: The protocol has five steps. One: the fact, without interpretation. Two: automatic thought, in quotes. Three: your certainty, from zero to a hundred, to practice calibration. Four: the mirror question, to train the open mind. Five: a rule for tomorrow, like if it happens again, then I'll do such a thing. The basis: A 2006 meta-analysis by Joanne Frattaroli of 146 studies found a small but real effect of writing about

licoes.r: Genesis 6–9 narrates a judgment by water: Earth filled with violence; Noah builds an ark; animals enter; it rains forty days; waters prevail a hundred fifty days; they cover “all the high mountains”; the ark rests; a new beginning with covenant and rainbow. The text speaks of fifteen cubits above the mountains (Gen 7:20), fountains of the great deep and windows of heaven. This theme does not mock faith: it asks, with public math and evidence, whether a literal global physical flood holds.
licoes.a: Details used in the following calculations: cubit ≈ 45.7 cm; Everest 8,849 m; 40 days of rain; ~150 days prevailing; about a year in the narrative until exit; ark 300×50×30 cubits; eight people; animals in pairs and, in places, seven pairs of clean animals. Internal tensions (40 vs 150 days; one pair vs seven) match interwoven sources (J/P). Practice: read Gen 6–9 once and mark what is number, dialogue, or theology.

licoes.t: Where would the water to cover Everest come from?
licoes.r: To cover Everest plus fifteen cubits, the water height is about 8,856 m. In a simplified uniform shell over Earth's whole surface (≈5.1×10⁸ km²), the extra volume is on the order of 4.5×10⁹ km³—about 3.4× all ocean water and hundreds of thousands of times atmospheric water. There is no known reservoir for that water, nor a physical place for it to go afterward.
licoes.a: Formula: V≈A×H with H=8849+15×0.457 m. Declared simplification: we do not model every valley; the order of magnitude already exceeds surface and atmospheric stocks. “Fountains of the deep” at that scale bring lethal heat and volume. Offline calculator: conteudo/calculadora-diluvio.html.

licoes.t: Forty days of rain and condensation heat
licoes.r: If ~8,856 m fell in 40 days, the average rate would be ~221 m/day ≈ 9,200 mm/h worldwide. World 24-hour rainfall records are near ~1,800 mm/day—orders of magnitude lower. Condensing ~4.5×10²¹ kg of water releases latent heat Q=m·L_v ≈10²⁸ J. Put into the atmosphere alone, that implies a ΔT of millions of kelvin—absurd for life.
licoes.a: Even spreading Q across all ocean mass yields a devastating global thermal jump. The problem is energy as well as source. See the calculator for formulas.

licoes.t: The ark: wood, space, food, manure, and eight people
licoes.r: With a 45.7 cm cubit, the ark is ~137×23×14 m (~43,000 m³ gross). The largest well-documented wooden ship (Wyoming schooner, ~100 m hull) already flexed and leaked. Counting only modern vertebrates (~37,000 species) with one pair, plus seven pairs for a “clean” fraction, yields tens of thousands of individuals—still without insects. Food, fresh water, manure, and ammonia with “one window” (Gen 6:16) and eight caretakers do not add up.
licoes.a: Orders of magnitude: ~0.5 kg food/animal/day → hundreds of tonnes/year. Task rates per person become impossible. Adjust species and rations in the calculator.

licoes.t: How would the kangaroo reach the ark—and return only to Australia?
licoes.r: Kangaroos and koalas live in Australia; sloths in South America; penguins and polar bears at the poles. Reaching the Near East means thousands of kilometers and oceans. Koalas need eucalyptus. Afterward, marsupials would have to return and remain only in Australia—opposite of the record. Two individuals per species imply a genetic bottleneck not seen as a single global funnel ~4,350 years ago.
licoes.a: Even miraculous rafting fails on diet, travel time, and repopulation. The calculator estimates a hypothetical overland travel time to show the premise’s absurdity.

licoes.t: Chronology, civilizations, and what Earth recorded
licoes.r: Ussher-style chronologies place the flood near 2348 BCE. Egypt’s Old Kingdom, Sumer, the Indus, and China show continuity—no global hiatus. Ice cores with >100 kyr of annual layers, varves, tree rings, and reefs lack a single recent global flood bed. Eight people repopulating Earth to known historical numbers needs impossible demography and would erase observed genetic diversity.
licoes.a: A recent global flood predicts global mud, synchronous extinction, a genetic funnel, civilizational collapse. That pattern is not what we see. Regional floods are.

licoes.t: What matches: local floods and Near Eastern myths
licoes.r: Flood deposits at sites such as Shuruppak/Ur (~2900 BCE) and Euphrates floods are real local catastrophes. Atrahasis, Gilgamesh XI, and Ziusudra tell boat-and-water stories older than Genesis’s final form. Inside Gen 6–9, traditions mix (40 vs 150 days; one pair vs seven): J/P literary stitching. The Black Sea hypothesis remains debated.
licoes.a: Reading Genesis beside Gilgamesh XI situates the text in a Near Eastern family of narratives. Many theologians accept that and still pray with the text.

licoes.t: How could millions of animal species fit in such a small ark?
p: millions of animals on the ark
licoes.r: This is where a literal reading is squeezed hardest. With a 45.7 cm cubit, the ark is ~137×23×14 m — gross volume ≈ 43,000 m³ (≈ 43 million liters). Land vertebrates described today alone (mammals ~6,400, birds ~11,000, reptiles ~12,000, amphibians ~8,000 → ~37,400 species), applying Genesis 7:2–3 (seven pairs of clean animals and of birds; one pair of the others), exceed ~200,000 individuals. That is ~0.18 m³ per animal — about 180 liters — for body, a year of food, water, and movement, averaging elephant and hummingbird together. Add described terrestrial biota including insects (~1.3–1.5 million species) or the ~8.7 million species estimate (Mora et al. 2011) minus ~2.2 million marine (~6.5 million terrestrial), and “space” falls to a few liters or ~2 liters each. This is geometry, not mockery. As literal global history it does not add up; as a religious narrative inspired by real local floods and older myths, the ark’s size works as symbol, not as a planetary cargo ship.
licoes.a: Three tiers in the Flood Calculator (Ark capacity mode): (A) land vertebrates only ~37k species → ~200k+ animals → ~0.18 m³/animal; (B) described terrestrial species incl. insects ~1.4M → millions of individuals → ~9 L/animal; (C) ~8.7M total minus ~2.2M marine → ~6.5M terrestrial → tens of millions of individuals → ~2 L/animal. Add food, water, manure, and care by 8 people. Sources: vertebrate catalogs/IUCN; Mora et

licoes.t: Animal journeys: continents, oceans, and the return home
licoes.r: Read as literal global transport to the Ararat region (~39.7°N 44.3°E), each biome requires a trip biology does not allow. Kangaroo, koala, wombat from Australia (~11–13k km) with the Indian Ocean in the way — koalas need Australian eucalyptus. Sloth, armadillo, llama from South America (~11–13k km) across the Atlantic; sloths move ~0.2 km/h. Antarctic penguins and Arctic polar bears need ice and cold-water prey — incompatible with Anatolian highlands. Madagascar lemurs (~6,500 km) do not cross the Mozambique Channel (~400 km of sea). Galápagos tortoises and New Zealand kiwi are island endemics. North American bison (~10k km) still face the Atlantic. Even when continuous land travel would take dozens or thousands of days, the decisive barrier is the ocean. Returning only to the home continent requires the same miracle twice. Extinct species would add to the cast, not shrink it. As literal history: ❌. As religious narrative with symbolic animals / local floods: fits the genre.
licoes.a:
Use Calculator → Journeys mode. Also checkable: dove/olive after ~1 year under seawater (❌/⚠️); Noah at 600 and family of 8 (genetic bottleneck); Gen 6:3 120 years; Gen 7:11–8:14 chronology; raven; sacrifice of clean animals after landing; carnivores' food after disembarking.

Quotations: Genesis 8:4 (King James Version): “And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountain

licoes.t: The portrait of God in the flood story
licoes.r: We do not judge anyone's sincere faith, and we do not diagnose God, Noah, or the authors. Psychology/psychiatry cannot diagnose literary characters or deity — say that plainly. We can rigorously read the portrait the text paints: a transparent balance of acts attributed to God in Gen 6–9, then compare with human ethics and how different readers answer. Acts in the text: decide to destroy humans and animals (Gen 6:7), including children and animals with no narrated guilt; 'regretted' making humankind (Gen 6:6); flood; then Gen 8:21 'I will not again curse the ground…' while admitting the human heart is still evil; covenant/rainbow (Gen 9). If a human ruler did the same, ethics would speak of collective and disproportionate punishment — not a psychiatric label. Eternal hell is NOT in this text (see the app's hell lessons). Readings: Jewish midrash (120 years as call to repent); Christian theodicy/allegory; progressive scholarship; critics (e.g. Ehrman, God's Problem); Mesopotamian Atrahasis background. Mestre Solar: the 'cruel God' image says more about ancient authors' worldview than about the divine; question fear-based images of God without mocking believers.
licoes.a: Calculator → Portrait / coherence mode. Logic table: omniscience vs regret; love vs collective destruction; omnipotence vs a flood that doesn't fix the heart (Gen 8:21); later eternal punishment vs finite acts. Epicurean trilemma (Lactantius)/Hume; replies: Plantinga free-will defense; Hick soul-making; symbolic reading; open theism; annihilationism/universalism — and why critics find them insufficient. Verdict: logi

licoes.t: A lie repeated many times — and the right to ask
licoes.r:
In Mestre Solar's words: a lie — or an unexamined story — repeated many times can become “truth” in a person's mind, rooted in the subconscious, rarely questioned. This is not an insult to believers: it is cognitive psychology.

Science names the **illusory truth effect**: repetition increases perceived truth even when people know better (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977; Fazio et al., 2015). Nearby: processing fluency; belief perseverance; childhood repetition plus authority.

The famous saying often blamed on Goebbels is **not documented** as his — treat it as a popular, misattributed proverb.

Gently tied to the flood: many heard Genesis 6–9 from childhood as settled fact. Examining verses, physics, and Near Eastern parallels is not a duty to abandon faith — it is the right not to let fear or habit think for you. Invite: question with calm, not fear. Sincere faith can bear light.
licoes.a: Hasher et al. 1977; Fazio et al. 2015; Quote Investigator on the misattribution. Return to the Calculator and “Think together.”

licoes.r: Portal verdict: water volume ❌; rain and latent heat ❌; fountains of the deep ❌; pressure/oxygen and salinity ❌; ark structure and logistics ❌; biogeography and pair genetics ❌; Ussher chronology vs civilizations and layered geology ❌. Local Mesopotamian floods ✅; Atrahasis/Gilgamesh/Ziusudra parallels ✅; J/P stitching ✅; Black Sea ⚠️. Overall: a literal global flood as physical reportage of Genesis 6–9 does not hold. That does not license mocking believers: many read it as theological narrative about violence, covenant, and restart, echoing real floods and older myths. Lying about Earth’s physics does not strengthen faith; honesty does.
licoes.a: Open the Flood Calculator (conteudo/calculadora-diluvio.html), vary height, rain days, and species, and watch the formulas. If your faith is literalist, this will sting—and the Portal prefers true discomfort to false comfort.

licoes.r: The app includes an offline Flood Calculator in the Portal’s gray-gold theme: conteudo/calculadora-diluvio.html. Choose target height (default Everest+15 cubits), rain days, cubit, species/pairs, and food per animal. It returns water volume vs oceans, mm/h vs record, heat and ΔT, ark volume per animal, food/water/manure per day, workload, and hypothetical kangaroo travel time. Formulas shown. Labels PT/EN/ES.
licoes.a: The calculator neither “proves God” nor “destroys God.” It turns physical claims into arithmetic. Águia Primordial remains the Portal voice; this new theme has no dedicated Águia recording yet—device voice may read until audio exists.

licoes.t: What the Adam and Eve story tells (Genesis 1–5)
licoes.r: Genesis 1 tells of creation in six days, ending with man and woman created together (Gen 1:27: “male and female created he them”). Genesis 2 tells it again: man is formed from dust (Gen 2:7), placed in Eden, and woman is made from a rib (Gen 2:22). In Genesis 3 a talking serpent persuades the woman to eat the forbidden fruit (Gen 3:6); curses and expulsion follow (Gen 3:23). Genesis 4–5 continue with Cain, Abel and lifespans over 900 years. This theme does not mock faith: it checks each detail against science and against the text itself, verse in hand.
licoes.a:
How to read this theme: every claim comes with its verse quoted right there and with the scientific source. At the end there is a table of what matches, what doesn't and what can't be verified. Practice: read Genesis 1 to 5 in one go and note what is a number, what is the order of events and what is teaching.

Citations (check the text): Genesis 1:1 (King James Version, public domain): “In the beginning God created t

licoes.r: Genesis marks days with evening and morning (Gen 1:5: “And the evening and the morning were the first day”) and ends the work on the seventh day (Gen 2:2). Science measures another scale: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, from radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest rocks — source: https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/geotime/age.html. The universe is about 13.8 billion years old. The sum: 6 days versus about 1.6 trillion days for Earth alone.
licoes.a: How radiometric dating works: certain atoms (uranium, potassium) turn into others at a constant rate measured in the lab. Like an hourglass, the ratio between what is left and what formed tells how long ago the rock closed. Different methods in different labs reach the same age — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiometric_dating. Some read the 'days' as ages. Even so, the order of events doesn't match, as the

licoes.t: The order of creation vs the fossil record
licoes.r: Genesis 1 gives an order: light on day 1 (Gen 1:3), fruit trees on day 3 (Gen 1:11), Sun and stars only on day 4 (Gen 1:16), fish, great sea creatures and birds on day 5 (Gen 1:20–21), land animals on day 6 (Gen 1:24). The fossil record shows another: the Sun (≈4.6 billion years) comes before Earth — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun; land animals (≈370 million, like Tiktaalik) come before birds (≈150 million, descended from dinosaurs) — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_of_birds; fruiting plants only ≈130 million — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowering_plant; and whales came from land mammals ≈50 million years ago — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolution_of_cetaceans.
licoes.a:
Real order, summarised: Sun → Earth → sea life (≈3.5 billion) → land plants (≈470 million) → land vertebrates (≈370 million) → dinosaurs → birds (≈150 million) → flowering plants (≈130 million) → whales (≈50 million) → Homo sapiens (≈300,000). One point matches: humans came last. The others don't.

licoes.t: Genesis 1 vs Genesis 2: two different orders
licoes.r: Side by side. Genesis 1: plants (Gen 1:11) → animals (Gen 1:24) → man and woman together, last (Gen 1:27: “male and female created he them”). Genesis 2: no plant of the field yet (Gen 2:5) → man is formed (Gen 2:7) → God makes trees grow (Gen 2:9) → forms the animals and brings them to the man (Gen 2:19: “out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field... and brought them unto Adam”) → finally woman, from the rib (Gen 2:22). In chapter 1 man comes after the animals; in 2, before. In 1 the couple is created together; in 2, separately.
licoes.a: Why: the most accepted scholarly explanation is that Genesis joins two accounts of different origins. Genesis 1 ('Priestly', P) uses 'God' (Elohim), orderly and solemn; Genesis 2 ('Yahwist', J) uses 'LORD God' (YHWH Elohim) and is a story with God shaping clay — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary_hypothesis. Defenders of a single reading say Gen 2 only 'details' Gen 1, but the order of events is still

licoes.t: A single first couple? What genetics says
licoes.r: The text says Eve “was the mother of all living” (Gen 3:20). Population genetics measures the variety in our DNA and calculates how many people were needed to produce it: the ancestral population never fell below a few thousand individuals (estimates around 10,000) — source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature10231. One couple cannot carry that much variation. Our DNA also holds pieces inherited from Neanderthals and Denisovans — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interbreeding_between_archaic_and_modern_humans.
licoes.a:
Correcting a common idea: 'Mitochondrial Eve' and 'Y-chromosome Adam' were not a couple. They lived at different times, tens of thousands of years apart depending on the study, and each lived among thousands of other people whose genes also reached us through other parts of the DNA — sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondrial_Eve and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y-chromosomal_Adam.

Citations (check the te

licoes.t: From dust and rib vs biology
licoes.r: The text: “the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground” (Gen 2:7) and “the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman” (Gen 2:22). What matches as an image: the body is made of common elements (carbon, oxygen, calcium). What doesn't: humans arose by gradual evolution; Homo sapiens is ≈300,000 years old (Jebel Irhoud fossils, Morocco) — source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature22336 — and we share about 98–99% of comparable DNA with chimpanzees — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimpanzee_genome_project.
licoes.a:
Correcting a popular myth: men do NOT have one rib fewer. Men and women have 12 pairs — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rib_cage. Even if a father lost a rib, it would not pass to his children: acquired traits are not inherited. Biologically there is no path to build an adult person from a bone.

Citations (check the text): Genesis 2:7 (King James Version, public domain): “And the LORD God formed man of the dus

licoes.t: The talking serpent, 'eating dust' and the tree of life
licoes.r: The serpent talks and argues (Gen 3:1) and is cursed: “upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life” (Gen 3:14). Biology: snakes have no vocal cords or a brain capable of language — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake; all are carnivores, none eats dust; and fossils show snakes with little hind legs ≈95 million years ago (Najash), losing their legs gradually long before people existed — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Najash. The tree of life (Gen 2:9; 3:22) and the cherubim with a flaming sword (Gen 3:24) are supernatural claims: not verifiable.
licoes.a: Context: a 'plant of life' stolen by a serpent also appears in the Epic of Gilgamesh, a Mesopotamian poem older than Genesis — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh. Winged guardians at sacred entrances (lamassu) were common in the region's art — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamassu. These are cultural parallels, not proof of direct copying. Note: in Genesis the serpent is not called Satan;

licoes.t: Death before sin? What fossils show
licoes.r: The traditional reading says death entered the world through sin: “by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin” (Romans 5:12), linked to Gen 2:17 and 3:19 (“dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return”). Fossils show billions of years of life and death before any human: stromatolites ≈3.5 billion years old, five mass extinctions (the dinosaurs' 66 million years ago) — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extinction_event — and even bone cancer in a ≈76-million-year-old dinosaur — source: https://doi.org/10.1016/S1470-2045(20)30171-6.
licoes.a:
More evidence: predators with hunting teeth, bones with bite marks, fossil prey inside predators, disease in ancient bones (paleopathology) — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleopathology. Death, disease and predation are far older than humanity. Some Christian readings take the 'death' of Genesis as spiritual, not physical; that's theology and does not change the fossils.

Citations (check the text): Genesis

licoes.t: Cain: his wife, the city and whom he feared
licoes.r: After killing Abel, Cain fears: “every one that findeth me shall slay me” (Gen 4:14). Who, if only Adam, Eve and he existed? He goes to the land of Nod (Gen 4:16) and “Cain knew his wife... and he builded a city” (Gen 4:17). The text doesn't say where the wife came from. A city needs many people; the first real cities, like Uruk, appear ≈6,000 years ago in societies of thousands — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruk. In the same line, Abel is a shepherd and Cain a farmer (Gen 4:2), and Tubal-cain already makes tools 'of brass and iron' (Gen 4:22): in real history, farming begins ≈11,500 years ago and large-scale iron ≈3,200 — sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age.
licoes.a:
The traditional answer: Adam had 'sons and daughters' (Gen 5:4), and Cain would have married a sister. But that isn't in chapter 4, and it doesn't explain whom Cain feared or who populated a city. The simplest reading is that the story assumes, without saying, that other people existed — which fits genetics, not a single couple.

licoes.r: Genesis 5 gives ages: “all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years” (Gen 5:5); Methuselah 969 (Gen 5:27). The longest documented human life is 122 years (Jeanne Calment, 1875–1997) — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Calment. Adding up the genealogies, Archbishop James Ussher (1650) dated creation to 4004 BC, about 6,000 years ago — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ussher_chronology. licoes.t: Where the story comes from: two sources and Mesopotamian myths
licoes.r: Scholars explain the repetitions in Genesis 1–2 as two joined sources: the Priestly (P) in Genesis 1 and the Yahwist (J) in Genesis 2–3 — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary_hypothesis. And there are parallels with older Mesopotamian texts: in Enuma Elish the world arises from divided primordial waters and humanity is made to serve the gods (compare 'the deep' and 'the waters', Gen 1:2) — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/En%C3%BBma_Eli%C5%A1; in Atrahasis humans are shaped from clay mixed with divine blood (compare Gen 2:7) — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atra-Hasis; in the Adapa myth a man loses the chance to eat the food of eternal life — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adapa; and in Gilgamesh a serpent steals the plant that renewed youth (compare Gen 3:22) — source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh.
licoes.a:
Honest caution: these are parallels, not proof of copying. The Hebrew authors lived in the same cultural world and seem to have answered those stories with their own theology: one God, humans with the dignity of the 'image of God', no war among gods. That shows Genesis as human literature in dialogue with its time.

In the scientific sum, 20 of 26 claims don't match (six days, order of creation, single couple, rib, talking serpent, death only after sin, 930 years, a 6,000-year-old world), 4 match and 2 are not verifiable. licoes.t: Who created the God of the Bible? The question and the method
licoes.r: This theme's question: does the God described in the Bible look more like a loving divine being, or like the mindset of the people who wrote about him, in a specific time and place? The same book says “Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;” (Exodus 20:5) and also “He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.” (1 John 4:8). Two: controlling people was one function of these texts, but not the only one. They also gave a small people an identity, explained wars and disasters, and held the group together in exile. licoes.t: Who wrote the Bible: many hands, many centuries
licoes.r: Tradition says Moses wrote the first five books, but the text itself narrates his death (Deut 34). Since the 19th century, scholars have identified distinct sources with their own style, names for God and interests. The classic labels are J (Yahwist), E (Elohist), D (Deuteronomist) and P (Priestly), in the documentary hypothesis popularized by Richard Friedman's 'Who Wrote the Bible?' (1987). Many today prefer supplementary models, where a base text receives layers over time. A landmark is “And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.” (2 Kings 22:8): King Josiah (c. 622 BC) 'finds' a law book, which most scholars link to the core of Deuteronomy, written or revised to support his religious and political reform.
licoes.a: The P layer and much of the final editing come from the Babylonian exile and after (6th–5th centuries BC). Genesis 1 is a priestly text, and even there a plural appears: “And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the eart

licoes.t: Where Yahweh came from: a storm god from the south
licoes.r: The name of God most used in the Hebrew Bible is YHWH (Yahweh). The oldest texts say he came from the south, from Seir, Edom and Teman, not from Israel: “And he said, The LORD came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir unto them; he shined forth from mount Paran, and he came with ten thousands of saints: from his right hand went a fiery law for them.” (Deuteronomy 33:2) And also “LORD, when thou wentest out of Seir, when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled, and the heavens dropped, the clouds also dropped water.” (Judges 5:4) Egyptian inscriptions from the 14th–13th centuries BC mention 'the Shasu of YHW', nomads of that region. So many scholars, like Thomas Römer in 'The Invention of God' (Harvard, 2015), think Yahweh began as a storm and war god of southern groups (Midianites or Kenites) and was only later adopted in Israel.
licoes.a: A telling detail: a storm and war god is described with thunder, fire, earthquake and victory in battle, exactly the imagery of many ancient texts about Yahweh (Judg 5:4–5; Ps 18; Hab 3:3). It is a well-grounded hypothesis, not a closed fact, and details are still debated. Sources: Yahweh — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahweh ; Kenite hypothesis — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenite_hypothesis ; Römer — https://www

licoes.t: El, Asherah and 'God's wife': the Canaanite pantheon
licoes.r: In the Ugaritic texts (c. 1300 BC, in today's Syria), the high god is El, his consort is Asherah, and they have 70 sons, the 'sons of El', each linked to a people. The Bible keeps echoes of this. The KJV has “When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel.” (Deuteronomy 32:8), but the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint read 'according to the number of the sons of God', which recalls El's 70 sons, one per nation. And the Psalm says: “God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.” (Psalms 82:1)
licoes.a: Archaeology confirms a goddess worshipped alongside Yahweh. At Kuntillet Ajrud (c. 800 BC), jars carry the blessing 'by Yahweh of Samaria and his Asherah'. The Bible shows people baking cakes for the 'queen of heaven': “The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead their dough, to make cakes to the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto other gods, that they may provoke

licoes.t: From many gods to one: monotheism is born in exile
licoes.r: The oldest texts don't deny that other gods exist. They demand that Israel serve Yahweh alone. That is monolatry: “For thou shalt worship no other god: for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God:” (Exodus 34:14) The Bible names neighboring gods plainly: “Because that they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon, and have not walked in my ways, to do that which is right in mine eyes, and to keep my statutes and my judgments, as did David his father.” (1 Kings 11:33) Full monotheism, the idea that only one God exists, emerges strongly in Second Isaiah, written during the Babylonian exile (c. 540 BC): “I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, though thou hast not known me:” (Isaiah 45:5)
licoes.a: Why in exile? Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed in 586 BC. A defeated people had two options: accept that Babylon's gods were stronger, or say Yahweh himself had used Babylon to punish Israel. The scribes chose the second. So Yahweh became responsible for everything, even evil: “I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the LORD do all these things.” (Isaiah 45:7) This is the root

licoes.t: The warrior God and the kings of the ancient Near East
licoes.r: How Yahweh acts in war was the standard of the age. On the Mesha Stele (c. 840 BC, Louvre), the king of Moab says his god Chemosh ordered him to attack Nebo, and that he killed its 7,000 inhabitants, men, women and girls, because he had 'devoted them to destruction' (the same idea as the biblical 'herem'). The Bible itself tells of the war against this king and says that when he sacrificed his son, “Then he took his eldest son that should have reigned in his stead, and offered him for a burnt offering upon the wall. And there was great indignation against Israel: and they departed from him, and returned to their own land.” (2 Kings 3:27)
licoes.a: Deuteronomy also copies the form of Assyrian vassal treaties. Esarhaddon's succession treaty (672 BC) required reporting even one's own relative who conspired against the king, and lists curses such as eating the flesh of one's own children. Here are the texts as they are, in full. Next to each, how the same order would be judged today under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998).

1) Numbers 31, after the war against Midian, Moses says: “Now therefore kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman that hath known man by lying with him.” (Numbers 31:17) “But all the women children, that have not known a man by lying with him, keep alive for yourselves.” (Numbers 31:18) Today: genocide (art. 6), killing prisoners and children (art. 8) and sexual slavery (arts. 7.1.g and 8.2.b.xxii).

2) “But of the cities of these people, which the LORD thy God doth give thee for an inheritance, thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth:” (Deuteronomy 20:16) “But thou shalt utterly destroy them; namely, the Hittites, and the Amorites, the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites; as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee:” (Deuteronomy 20:17) Today: genocide (art. 6) and an order of 'no survivors', a war crime (art. 8.2.b.xii).

3) “Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.” (1 Samuel 15:3) Today: genocide (art. 6) and intentional attack on civilians (art. 8.2.b.i).

4) At Jericho: “And they utterly destroyed all that was in the city, both man and woman, young and old, and ox, and sheep, and ass, with the edge of the sword.” (Joshua 6:21) Today: genocide and a crime against humanity (arts. 6 and 7).

5) “And it came to pass, that at midnight the LORD smote all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sat on his throne unto the firstborn of the captive that was in the dungeon; and all the firstborn of cattle.” (Exodus 12:29) Today: collective punishment of children for a ruler's decision, banned by Geneva Convention IV (art. 33).

6) The flood: “And every living substance was destroyed which was upon the face of the ground, both man, and cattle, and the creeping things, and the fowl of the heaven; and they were destroyed from the earth: and Noah only remained alive, and they that were with him in the ark.” (Genesis 7:23) Today: extermination (art. 7.1.b).
licoes.a:
Behaviour traits these texts describe, without diagnosis: collective punishment (the innocent pay for the group), dehumanization of the other people (all become 'enemies' to destroy) and sparing only virgins treated as spoils. Diagnosing a literary character is neither possible nor honest. What can be said is: a human giving these orders today would stand trial for war crimes.
