licoes.t: A God in the image of those who describe him: what psychology says
licoes.r: You cannot diagnose a character in a book; doing so would be as unscientific as calling him perfect. But patterns can be compared. The traits the texts give Yahweh match the ideals of an ancient Near Eastern warrior king: jealousy and a demand for exclusive loyalty (“Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;” (Exodus 20:5)), total destruction of the enemy (“And when the LORD thy God shall deliver them before thee; thou shalt smite them, and utterly destroy them; thou shalt make no covenant with them, nor shew mercy unto them:” (Deuteronomy 7:2)), collective punishment and reward for the obedient. Modern psychology studies these patterns in people and groups: dehumanization of the out-group (Nick Haslam, 2006), moral disengagement, which is justifying violence by a 'higher' cause (Albert Bandura), and collective punishment.
licoes.a: And there is direct experimental data: in 2009 Nicholas Epley and colleagues (PNAS) showed that when religious people estimate what God thinks about controversial issues, the answer tracks their own opinion more than the opinion they attribute to others. When their own view shifted, their 'God' shifted with it. A modern hint of something ancient: each generation tends to describe God with its own mind. This fits your

licoes.t: From Sheol to hell: how eternal punishment was built
licoes.r: For almost the entire Old Testament there is no hell of torment. The dead go to Sheol, a dark, silent place for everyone, good and bad: “For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten.” (Ecclesiastes 9:5) “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.” (Ecclesiastes 9:10) And the psalmist asks: “For in death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?” (Psalms 6:5) The first clear mention of different fates after death only appears in Daniel, written around 165 BC: “And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.” (Daniel 12:2)
licoes.a: Between the exile and the time of Jesus, Judaism came into contact with Persian Zoroastrianism (final judgment, resurrection, cosmic battle of good and evil) and with Greek culture (immortal soul, Hades and Tartarus). The idea of punishment grew in that mix. The gospels have “Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:” (M

licoes.t: Gods who watch and punish: religion and social control
licoes.r: Your intuition that religion served to control has a scientific basis, but the story is fuller. Psychologist Ara Norenzayan, in 'Big Gods' (Princeton, 2013), proposes that all-seeing, punishing gods helped large societies cooperate among strangers: people who feel watched cheat less. A study across 8 societies (Purzycki et al., Nature, 2016) found more generosity toward distant co-religionists among those who believed in a moralizing, punishing god. In the Bible the formula is explicit: obedience brings blessing, and disobedience brings “I also will do this unto you; I will even appoint over you terror, consumption, and the burning ague, that shall consume the eyes, and cause sorrow of heart: and ye shall sow your seed in vain, for your enemies shall eat it.” (Leviticus 26:16) and “But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee:” (Deuteronomy 28:15)
licoes.a: Scientific honesty: in 2019 a famous Nature study (Whitehouse et al.) claimed societies became complex before moralizing gods appeared. It was criticized for treating missing data as 'absence' (Beheim et al., Nature, 2021) and was retracted. The debate remains open. What is known: belief in a watching, punishing god increases cooperation and obedience within the group, and rulers can use that. But religion also gave

licoes.t: 'God is love' vs the texts: contradictions that invite questions
licoes.r: The Bible also says “He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.” (1 John 4:8), “The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.” (Psalms 145:9), “Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.” (Luke 6:36) and “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Micah 6:8) And it contradicts itself on inherited guilt. Exodus says “Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;” (Exodus 20:5), but Ezekiel answers “The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.” (Ezekiel 18:20) These voices don't fit the massacre orders in the previous lessons. That is what you'd expect from a book written by many people, in different eras, with different ideas about God.
licoes.a: How believers handle this, to be fair: in the 2nd century Marcion concluded the Old Testament God was a different god, and was declared a heretic. Origen read the massacres as allegories of inner struggle. Today apologists like Paul Copan ('Is God a Moral Monster?', 2011) say the texts use typical ancient war hyperbole, and theologians speak of 'progressive revelation'. Notice that all these answers admit that, read

licoes.t: How a repeated idea becomes 'truth': the illusory truth effect
licoes.r: In 1977 Lynn Hasher and colleagues showed that statements heard several times seem truer than new ones, even when false. This is the illusory truth effect. In 2015 Lisa Fazio and colleagues showed it works even when people know the right answer: repetition creates familiarity, and the brain mistakes familiarity for truth. Add three reinforcers: hearing it from childhood from people we love; seeing adults make costly sacrifices for the faith (anthropologist Joseph Henrich calls these CREDs, 2009); and fear of questioning, when doubt is treated as sin and leaving can cost your family (compare “If thy brother, the son of thy mother, or thy son, or thy daughter, or the wife of thy bosom, or thy friend, which is as thine own soul, entice thee secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods, which thou hast not known, thou, nor thy fathers;” (Deuteronomy 13:6)).
licoes.a: This explains why intelligent, good people believe sincerely. They weren't foolish: they received a story repeated for generations, in an environment that rewarded accepting and punished doubting. A fair point: the effect applies to all of us, to any idea, including our own. The antidote is the same for any belief: go to the source, compare versions, ask 'how would I know if this were false?'. Sources: illusory truth

licoes.r: Verdict: the image of God in the Bible was written by human beings, and that matches reality. Many hands over about a thousand years: tribes with a storm god from the south, kings who needed loyalty, priests in exile who turned defeat into 'punishment for sins', and later teachers who, under Persian and Greek influence, created eternal hell. This God's harshest traits (jealousy, exclusive loyalty, collective punishment, extermination of the enemy) are those of the kings and war gods of the age, as on the Mesha Stele and in Assyrian treaties. A human giving the orders of Numbers 31 or 1 Samuel 15 today would be tried for genocide. And the same book also says 'God is love' and 'the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father'. They are different human voices that don't agree with each other.

licoes.r: This theme completes what the Portal has already shown, without repeating it. Already covered elsewhere: the six days, Genesis 1 × Genesis 2, the single couple and genetics, the rib, the serpent and biology, Cain's wife and the 930 years (theme 'Adam and Eve'); the ark and the water (theme 'The math of the flood'); who wrote the Bible, where Yahweh came from and the illusory truth effect (theme 'Who created the God of the Bible?'); and dozens of contradictions (theme 'Contradictions, atrocities and manipulation'). Here come the missing pieces: why an all-knowing God asks questions, how the serpent became Satan, why there are talking animals, what the text doesn't explain about Cain and Abel, whether God or people wrote the Bible, and why children accept what they hear as absolute truth.
licoes.a: The method is the same for each point, step by step: 1) what the text says, with the full verse; 2) what science, history and archaeology show; 3) what is myth, meaning a narrative that conveys meaning but doesn't describe facts; 4) what still has value. Myth here is not an insult: it is a literary genre, like the fable or the parable. At the end comes a summary table with what matches reality, what doesn't and what

licoes.t: Why does an all-knowing God ask questions?
licoes.r: Right after the fruit, the text says “And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9). And goes on: “And he said, Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?” (Genesis 3:11). To the woman: “And the LORD God said unto the woman, What is this that thou hast done? And the woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.” (Genesis 3:13). With Cain, the same: “And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother’s keeper?” (Genesis 4:9). Yet another text in the same Bible says “For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether.” (Psalms 139:4). If God knows everything, why ask where someone is, or where the murdered brother is?
licoes.a: There are three main readings, and all deserve respect. 1) Historical reading: Genesis 2 to 4 comes from the source scholars call the Yahwist (J), which describes God in very human terms: he shapes clay, walks in the garden 'in the cool of the day' (Gen 3:8) and makes garments of skin (Gen 3:21). In this portrait, God really seems to find things out. Omniscience appears in other texts, like Psalm 139, and was systema

licoes.t: 'I will go down and see': the God who has to check
p: i will go down and see
now i know that you fear god
tower of babel god came down
licoes.r: Elsewhere, God seems to need to see in order to know. At the tower of Babel: “And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men builded.” (Genesis 11:5). About Sodom: “I will go down now, and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry of it, which is come unto me; and if not, I will know.” (Genesis 18:21). And after ordering Abraham to sacrifice his son: “And he said, Lay not thine hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him: for now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me.” (Genesis 22:12). 'Now I know' implies that before, he did not.
licoes.a: The readings: Rashi, on Gen 18:21, reads 'I will go down' as a lesson for judges: do not decide life-and-death cases without first examining carefully. Classical theologians such as Boethius and Thomas Aquinas teach that God knows everything at once, outside time, and that these texts speak 'in human fashion'. Open theism, a modern Christian current, reads these passages more literally: free choices would not yet be

licoes.t: From serpent to Satan: how the snake became the devil
licoes.r: In Genesis, the serpent is an animal: “Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?” (Genesis 3:1). Its punishment is an animal's too: crawling and eating dust (Gen 3:14), and enmity between snakes and people: “And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.” (Genesis 3:15). The name Satan appears nowhere in Genesis. In the Hebrew Bible, 'satan' means 'adversary' or 'accuser', and appears as a member of the heavenly court: “Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them.” (Job 1:6). In Zechariah he accuses the high priest: “And he shewed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him.” (Zechariah 3:1). The link between the serpent and the devil appears centuries later: in the book of Wisdom (around the 1st century BC), 'by the envy of the devil, death came into the world' (Wis 2:24); and in the last book of the New Testament: “And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him.” (Revelation 12:9).
licoes.a: Why this matters: the story many learn as children ('Satan, disguised as a snake, deceived Eve') is a later reading laid over the text. Many scholars link the growth of the Satan figure to the period when Jews lived under the Persian Empire, whose religion (Zoroastrianism) had an evil spirit, Angra Mainyu, fighting the good god. This is a much-debated hypothesis, not a proven fact. Christians, from Irenaeus (2nd cent

licoes.t: Talking animals: the serpent, the donkey and ancient fables
licoes.r: The Bible has two talking animals: the serpent in Eden and Balaam's donkey: “And the LORD opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?” (Numbers 22:28). In biology this doesn't happen: speech requires a vocal apparatus able to articulate sounds and brain areas for language. Snakes have no vocal cords and only hiss; donkeys bray but don't form words. In the ancient world, though, the talking animal was a well-known storytelling device. In Egypt, the 'Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor', from the Middle Kingdom (about 4,000 years ago), has a giant serpent that talks with a sailor. And the fables attributed to Aesop (6th century BC) use talking animals to teach lessons.
licoes.a: In the Bible itself, the serpent has another curious role. Moses makes a bronze serpent that heals whoever looks at it: “And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.” (Numbers 21:9). Centuries later, King Hezekiah destroys it, because the people were burning incense to it: “He removed the high place

licoes.t: Cain and Abel: why was one offering accepted and not the other?
licoes.r: Abel offers animals from the flock and Cain, fruit of the ground: “And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering:” (Genesis 4:4) “But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.” (Genesis 4:5). The text doesn't explain why God preferred one offering. Explanations came later: the New Testament says “By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh.” (Hebrews 11:4) and “Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.” (1 John 3:12). Ancient interpreters noticed that Abel brought 'the firstlings' and 'the fat', and Cain only 'of the fruit', and concluded that Cain gave half-heartedly. Before the crime, God warns: “If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.” (Genesis 4:7). After the crime: “And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.” (Genesis 4:10).
licoes.a: Historical reading: many scholars see here the clash between two ways of life, the shepherd's and the farmer's, who lived side by side and competed for land and water in the Near East. There is a Sumerian poem, 'Dumuzid and Enkimdu', in which a shepherd and a farmer compete for the goddess Inana: she prefers the farmer, her brother speaks up for the shepherd, and in the end the two make peace. It is a thematic parall

licoes.t: The mark of Cain: from protection to an excuse for racism
licoes.r: In the text, the mark of Cain is a protection: “And the LORD said unto him, Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold. And the LORD set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill him.” (Genesis 4:15). Genesis doesn't say what the mark was and says nothing about skin color. Even so, from at least the 1730s in the United States, the idea spread that Black people descended from Cain and that dark skin was the 'curse'. This was used to justify slavery and discrimination. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, for example, did not ordain Black men from 1852 until 1978. Today it officially disavows the theory that black skin is a sign of a curse.
licoes.a: A detail that touches Brazil: the church itself says, in its official essay, that Black and mixed-ancestry members helped build the São Paulo temple, which they would not be allowed to enter, and that this weighed on the 1978 change. This is an example of how a reading called 'the word of God' can shield a human prejudice: the text didn't say it, but once placed as sacred it seemed beyond question. Something similar

licoes.t: Did God write the Bible, or did people write in God's name?
p: is the bible the word of god
licoes.r: The Bible itself shows people speaking in God's name, and admits that this could be false. Jeremiah accuses: “How do ye say, We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us? Lo, certainly in vain made he it; the pen of the scribes is in vain.” (Jeremiah 8:8) (modern translations: 'the false pen of the scribes has made it into a lie'). And also: “Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.” (Jeremiah 23:16). In other words, even then there were people saying 'thus says the Lord' with ideas from their own heads, and the text recognizes it. The formula wasn't unique to Israel: in the letters from the city of Mari, in Syria (around 1770 BC), prophets brought King Zimri-Lim messages beginning 'Thus says Dagan' or 'Thus says Adad', the gods there.
licoes.a: What history shows: the books were written by people, in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, over about a thousand years, and the list of books was decided gradually (see 'Who wrote the Bible' and 'Who chose the books of the Bible'). Other books also claim to come from God: the Quran, the Book of Mormon and the Vedas, called in India 'shruti', 'that which was heard'. They contradict one another, so the sentence 'this book cam

licoes.t: Why a 'sacred' book feels like absolute truth
licoes.r: When an idea is called sacred, the mind starts treating it differently. Psychologist Philip Tetlock (2003) described 'sacred values': things people refuse to weigh against anything else, and which provoke outrage at the mere thought of questioning them. Scott Atran and Jeremy Ginges (Science, 2012) showed that sacred values resist arguments and even material offers. That's why a text declared sacred stops being read as 'what someone wrote' and starts being read as 'what is'.
licoes.a: Three mechanisms combined: 1) authority: we learn from those we trust (parents, pastor, priest), and questioning feels like betrayal; 2) repetition: the illusory truth effect (theme 'Who created the God of the Bible?'); 3) the cost of doubting: fear of punishment and of losing family and community. The text sometimes protects itself: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought

licoes.t: Sponge mind: why children accept what they hear as truth
licoes.r: A child has no way to check alone whether God exists, whether the world is 6,000 years old or whether there is a hell. Children learn through adults' testimony. Paul Harris and Melissa Koenig (Child Development, 2006) showed that children learn scientific things they can't see (the Earth is round, germs exist) and religious things (God, heaven) in the same way: by trusting the speaker. In a 2015 study, Kathleen Corriveau, Eva Chen and Paul Harris told stories to 5- and 6-year-olds. In religious stories with miracles, children who went to church or attended a religious school said the character was real; children from non-religious families said it was made up. The religious children also more often accepted fantastical stories as real.
licoes.a: This doesn't mean children believe anyone: from age 3 or 4 they prefer informants who were right before (Koenig and Harris, 2005). The point is different: when all the trusted adults say the same thing from early on, a child cannot know that it is one belief among many. Psychologist Daniel Gilbert (1991) showed that even in adults, understanding a sentence comes with believing it for a moment; doubting takes a second

licoes.t: If you had been born somewhere else: religion and birthplace
p: if i was born in another country
religion depends on where you are born
why do i follow my parents religion
licoes.r: The religion a person follows depends heavily on where and to whom they were born. In the Pew Research Center survey of 36 countries (published in 2025, nearly 80,000 people), in India, Israel, Nigeria and Thailand, 95% or more of adults remain in the religious group they were raised in. Even where switching is more common, most stay: in Brazil, 21% no longer identify with their childhood religion, so about 4 in 5 remain in it. Someone born into a Hindu family in India almost always stays Hindu; into a Jewish family in Israel, Jewish; into a Catholic or evangelical family in Brazil, most likely Christian.
licoes.a: Think it through: a boy born in Varanasi, India, to Hindu parents, grows up sure that Krishna is real; a boy born in Goiânia, Brazil, to evangelical parents, grows up sure that Jesus is the only way. Both are sincere, with the same kind of certainty, and each finds the other's belief strange. The sincerity is equal; what changes is the address. This doesn't prove that no religion is true, but it shows that the certai

licoes.t: Teaching to believe or teaching to think: the difference
licoes.r: Educating means teaching content and also how to evaluate it. Indoctrinating, according to philosopher of education I. A. Snook ('Indoctrination and Education', 1972), means teaching with the intention that the person believe regardless of the evidence. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) guarantees the child freedom of thought, conscience and religion (article 14), and says parents provide direction in a manner consistent with the child's evolving capacities.
licoes.a: In practice, the difference shows when a question comes. A child asks: 'Why did God ask where Adam was, if he knows everything?'. An answer that educates: 'Good question; there are several readings, let's look together'. An answer that indoctrinates: 'You don't question God's word'. The first shapes someone who thinks; the second, someone who obeys fear. The Bible has advice that fits here: “Prove all things; hold fa

licoes.r: This theme's sum: 24 claims checked, one per row, with verse and source. Result: ✅ 11 match reality, ❌ 10 don't and ❔ 3 are not verifiable. Matching: Satan as an accuser in the Hebrew Bible, the bronze serpent cult, the 'human' God of the oldest layer, the clash of shepherds and farmers, the racist use of verses, prophets speaking 'a vision of their own heart', the 'thus says the god' formula at Mari, the effect of the 'sacred' label, children's trust in adults and religion inherited from birth. Not matching: talking animals, snakes eating dust, the serpent as Satan in Genesis, a consistent text about an all-knowing God, Cain and Abel as humanity's second generation, the mark of Cain as dark skin and the idea that most people chose their religion by comparing. licoes.t: Conhecimento Solar's opinion: honest verdict on Genesis and belief
licoes.r: Verdict: as an account of facts, Genesis does not match reality. The talking serpent, the talking donkey, the snake that eats dust, Cain and Abel as humanity's second generation: none of it agrees with biology, genetics or archaeology. The text itself shows human hands: in one layer, a God who asks and comes down to see; in another, a God who knows everything; a serpent that became Satan only centuries later; and prophets who, according to Jeremiah, spoke 'a vision of their own heart'. Psychology explains why, even so, so many people feel these stories as absolute truth: they learned them in childhood, from people they loved, in a setting where the book was called sacred and doubting was dangerous. Had they been born in another country, they would feel the same certainty about another book.
licoes.a: Where care is needed: science neither proves nor refutes that God exists, nor that someone was inspired. What it shows is that the content of these texts reflects the knowledge and values of their writers, in an age without modern science. Myth is not garbage: Genesis carries deep questions about responsibility ('where art thou?'), guilt, envy and caring for one's brother. And sincere believers are not foolish: they

licoes.r: Co-creation is aligning intent, emotion and action. In spiritual traditions, you participate in the creation of your reality along with something greater. In practice, nothing is created without action.
licoes.a: Inner reading: cocreating is not giving orders to the universe, it's not fighting it. The Tao Te Ching calls it wu wei, the effortless, forced action, like water surrounding a stone. The Dhammapada opens like this: the mind precedes all things. Practice: Write down an intention today, feel it in your body for a minute, and take a single concrete action in that direction before you go to sleep.

licoes.r: The Law of Attraction says that like attracts like: thoughts and emotions would attract experiences. It comes from the 19th-century New Thought movement and was made famous by the 2006 film The Secret. There's no scientific proof that thinking alone attracts things.
licoes.a: Inner reading: what's real is that attention chooses what you see. He who searches for exits finds exits, persists more and does better. So the traditions speak of faith, but always along with works. Beware of the shadow of this idea: Never blame the sufferer for bringing his own pain. Practice: replace the request with the question, what step would I take today if I already trusted the path? And take the step.

licoes.r: Intention is the seed. A clear, written, repeated intention guides your attention, and attention guides your life.
licoes.a: Inner reading: In the tradition of the Upanishads it is said that you are your deepest desire, for as is the desire, so is the will, and as is the will, so is the act. Practice: Write the intention in the present, short and true, for example: I take care of my body every day. Read it when you wake up and when you sleep, and try it today with a little action.

licoes.r: Visualizing is practicing in your mind. Athletes have been using it for decades: the mind trains the path before the body. Studies show that visualizing the process and the obstacles works better than visualizing the trophy alone.
licoes.a: Inner reading: Psychologist Gabriele Oettingen called it mental contrast: imagine the wish fulfilled, then the most likely inner obstacle, and the plan for when it will appear. The alchemists spoke of true imagination, the imaginatio, as the force that gives form. Practice: close your eyes for two minutes, see the outcome, see the obstacle, and say, "If this happens, I'll do that".

licoes.r: Gratitude is the quickest shortcut to inner abundance. A grateful man sees what he already has.
licoes.a: Inner reading: Cicero wrote, in his Pro Plancio speech, that gratitude is not only the greatest of virtues, but the mother of all others. Gratitude shifts the center of the missing self to the receiving self. Research in positive psychology associates the habit of writing down gratitude with increased well-being. Practice: Tonight, write down three very specific things and in one of them, why it happened.

licoes.r: Affirmations are phrases that train the mind. They work best when they're believable to you and come with action. A 2009 study by Joanne Wood showed that exaggerated sentences can worsen the mood of those with low self-esteem.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the word only has power when the whole being agrees with it. If a statement sounds like a lie, the mind resists. In exchange I am rich because I am learning to take care of my money: a truth in the making convinces more than a fantasy. Practice: Write an affirmation that you can say by looking into your own eyes, in the mirror, without deviating.

licoes.r: In spiritual language, vibration is your inner state: what you feel and emanate. In physics, vibration is something else, measured in hertz, and the two should not be confused. There is no device that can measure the frequency of the soul.
licoes.a: Inner reading: what traditions call vibration is the quality of your presence. People feel when you're whole or divided. Raising the vibration, in practice, is taking care of sleep, body, company and thoughts. Practice: Before you enter a place today, take three breaths and choose the state you're going in.

licoes.r: Abundance starts as a mindset: seeing possibilities instead of just lack. But a mindset without strategy becomes just wishful thinking. Real prosperity comes from spending less than you earn, creating value and having patience.
licoes.a: Inside Reading: Jesus said, in Matthew six, where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. True poverty is when you never feel enough, even when you're full. Practice: Write down everything you spend for a week; abundance begins with clarity. And be wary of anyone who promises wealth in exchange for your money.

licoes.r: Detachment is not giving up. It's about acting with total dedication and letting go of control over the outcome. Buddhism teaches that much of suffering stems from attachment.
licoes.a: Inner reading: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says to Arjuna: You are entitled to action, but never to its fruits. This is not indifference, it is freedom: you do your best and do not enslave yourself to the result. Practice: pick something you control too much, an outcome, a person, an opinion, and do your part today and let go of the rest.

licoes.r: Hermeticism is a philosophical tradition attributed to the legendary Hermes Trismegistus. Its ancient texts, the Corpus Hermeticum, were written in Greek in Roman Egypt around the second and third centuries. The 1908 Caibalion summarizes seven principles: mentalism, correspondence, vibration, polarity, rhythm, cause and effect, and gender.
licoes.a: Important fact: The Caibalion is a modern book, signed by Three Initiates and usually attributed to William Walker Atkinson of New Thought. It's not a thousand-year-old Egyptian text. The Corpus Hermeticum, on the other hand, is ancient and speaks of something else: the mind, the Nous, which illuminates the human being so that he recognizes himself as coming from the divine. Practice: Read one principle a day and not

licoes.r: First principle of the Caibalion: Everything is Mind; the Universe is mental. For hermetics, reality arises from a universal consciousness.
licoes.a: Inner reading: Plotinus, in the third century, taught something similar, that everything emanates from the One through Intelligence, the Nous. In practice, the lesson is this: the way you think shapes the way you live, and psychology partly confirms that. On the other hand, the idea that the entire universe is mind is a philosophical assertion, not a proven one. Practice: Today, when a heavy thought comes, say to you

p: on earth as it is in heaven
assim na terra como no ceu
licoes.r: Second principle: what's above is like what's below. The phrase comes from the Emerald Tablet. There are patterns that repeat at various levels, from the individual to society.
licoes.a: Inside reading: the ancients spoke of the human being as a microcosm, a small universe that mirrors the big one. Use it as a mirror: Your outer world often reflects your inner world. It's a symbolic lens, not a law of physics. Practice: Clean up a small area of your home today and notice what's lining up inside you.

licoes.r: Principle three: nothing is stationary; everything moves; everything vibrates. Heraclitus, 500 years before Christ, taught that everything flows.
licoes.a: Honestly, in physics, atoms vibrate and particles are excitations of fields, but for different reasons and measured in the lab. Hermeticism uses this as a metaphor for mental states: raising the vibration is changing the inner state. Practice: When you feel a heavy state, move your body first, get up, walk, breathe, and watch your mind go along.

licoes.r: Fourth principle: everything is double; opposites are identical in nature and different in degree. Hot and cold are the same temperature in different degrees.
licoes.a: Inner reading: Heraclitus said that the way up and down is one. Fear and courage are the same energy at opposite poles: you don't eliminate fear, you move it, degree by degree. The hermetics called it mental transmutation. Practice: name what you're feeling right now and ask, what's the next degree, a little closer to the opposite pole?

licoes.r: Fifth principle: everything flows and flows back; everything has its tides. After the fall comes the climb. The book of Ecclesiastes says the same thing: There is an appointed time for everything.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the wise man neither deludes himself at the top nor despairs at the bottom. He knows that the pendulum turns and stays in the center. Caibalion calls it neutralizing the rhythm: not getting carried away by it. Practice: Today, when a wave comes, of euphoria or discouragement, say quietly: this too passes, and return to the center of the chest.

licoes.r: Sixth principle: every cause has an effect; chance is just an unknown law. Your choices today are tomorrow's crops.
licoes.a: Honesty: Karma, in Indian traditions, has various meanings and is not divine punishment; it is the law of action and its marks on the mind. That the universe returns every act is belief, not science. But taking ownership of one's choices is wisdom in any tradition. Heraclitus said: a man's character is his destiny. Practice: Before you make a decision today, ask yourself, what does this choice entail?

licoes.r: Seventh principle: gender is in everything; everything has a male and a female principle. This is not about biological sex, but about two forces: the one that designs and the one that welcomes and generates.
licoes.a: Inner reading: creating requires both. Whoever only acts burns out; whoever only receives stagnates. Taoism says something similar to yin and yang, and Jung spoke of the anima and animus within each person. Practice: If today you only pushed, stop and listen; if you only waited, take a step.

licoes.r: Quantum physics describes the world from the very small: atoms, electrons and light. It's one of the most tested theories in history, and from it came the laser, the transistor and the cell phone in your hand.
licoes.a: Deep reading: The most haunting is not what she promises, it's what she admits. Richard Feynman said in 1965: I think I can safely say that no one understands quantum mechanics. The theory works with absurd precision, but what it means, the so-called interpretations, are still up for debate. Honestly, a lot of what's sold as quantum healing, money and attraction has nothing to do with real physics. Practice: When you

licoes.r: In quantum physics, measuring a system changes what you observe. But observer, here, is any physical interaction of measurement, like a detector. It doesn't have to be a human mind.
licoes.a: This is the point most distorted by mysticism. Whether consciousness has any role in measurement is an open and minority question among physicists. Werner Heisenberg wrote, in Physics and Philosophy, 1958, that what we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning. Inner reading: the way you ask defines what you can see. Practice: In a difficult conversation today, change the question

licoes.r: In the double-slit experiment, electrons fired one by one form a wave pattern. If you measure which slit each one went through, the pattern disappears.
licoes.a: This shows that nature, at this scale, behaves neither like balls nor like ordinary waves. Feynman said that this experiment contains the only mystery of quantum physics. Inner reading: reality doesn't fit into our categories of this or that. Practice: Today, in front of someone you labeled, ask what that person is beyond the label.

licoes.r: Superposition is a system being in a combination of states until it is measured. Schrödinger's cat of 1935 was created precisely to show how absurd this seems on a human scale.
licoes.a: In large objects, interaction with the environment destroys the superposition very quickly; this is called decoherence. That's why you don't see live and dead cats at the same time. Inside reading: while you're undecided, all possibilities coexist, and indecision also comes at a price. Practice: Pick a small decision today that you've been putting off and make it.

licoes.r: Tangled particles have correlated outcomes, even at great distances. Einstein called it ghostly action at a distance. The experiments confirmed the phenomenon, and the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger for these tests.
licoes.a: Honesty: entanglement doesn't allow you to send messages faster than light, nor does it connect minds. Inside reading, as a metaphor and not as a physics: the universe is not made of isolated parts, and physicist David Bohm proposed an implicit order in which everything would be folded into the whole. It's an interpretation, not a consensus. Practice: think of someone far away today and make real contact.

licoes.r: For modern physics, vacuum is nothing: it's full of quantum fields, with small fluctuations of energy. That's measurable, like the Casimir effect.
licoes.a: But the quantum field is not a field of wishful thinking where you make requests to the universe; here poetry and physics separate. Inside reading: The Tao Te Ching, in chapter eleven, says it's the emptiness of the vessel that makes it useful. Practice: leave a blank space in your calendar today, unfilled, and see what comes of it.

licoes.r: Heisenberg's 1927 Uncertainty Principle says that one cannot know, at the same time and with complete precision, the position and motion of a particle. It is not a failure of the instruments: it is a property of nature.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the universe has limits to certainty, and humility is a form of wisdom. Socrates said something similar in the Apology: he was wiser only because he knew he didn't know. Practice: today, say I don't know at least once, without shame.

licoes.r: Some hypotheses, like that of Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff, suggest that consciousness involves quantum processes in the brain. It's a bold, unproven and highly contested hypothesis.
licoes.a: Most neuroscientists think the brain is too hot and humid to sustain delicate quantum effects. But the question remains open. Honest science says we don't know yet. Practice: when someone uses quantum consciousness to sell something, ask, what study, published where?

licoes.r: Quantum mysticism is using words from physics to sell spiritual ideas. Be wary of quantum healing, quantum wealth and quantum devices.
licoes.a: You can have spirituality without pretending it's physical. Feynman taught in 1974: the first principle is not to fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool. Truth needs no fantasy, and real science is haunting enough. Practice: separate, on a piece of paper, what you believe from experience and what you believe because someone sold you.

licoes.r: Discipline is choosing what you want most instead of what you want now. Start small, every day, no negotiation.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the word comes from disciple, one who learns. Discipline is not punishment, it's loyalty to yourself. Rule of thumb: never miss two days in a row; one bad day is an accident, two have become a habit. Practice: set a nonnegotiable minimum, so small you can't get away from it, and meet it today.

licoes.r: Focus is saying no to almost everything. One task at a time, cell phone away, twenty-five minutes without interruption: that's the Pomodoro technique.
licoes.a: The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. Where your attention goes, your life goes. Practice: Before you begin, write down the one thing you need to get ready, and work on it until the alarm goes off.

licoes.r: Stoicism teaches you to separate what depends on you from what doesn't. Take care of the first. Accept the second.
licoes.a: Epitetus, who was born a slave, wrote in the Manual: It is not the things that disturb men, but the judgments they make about them. Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome, wrote his Meditations for himself. Seneca reminded us that while we procrastinate, life passes. Practice: At night, like Seneca, review the day: what I did right, where I went wrong, what I'll do tomorrow.

licoes.r: Take a deep breath: four seconds to enter, four to hold, six to release. Repeat five times. If anxiety is frequent, seek medical attention.
licoes.a: Technique five, four, three, two, one: name five things you see, four you touch, three you hear, two you smell and one you taste. It brings the mind to the present. Inner reading: anxiety lives in the future; the body only exists now. If you're in distress, call 188, the CVV, free of charge, anytime.

p: what is the meaning of life
licoes.r: Purpose is not found ready; it is built. He lives where what you love meets what the world needs.
licoes.a: Viktor Frankl, a psychiatrist who survived Auschwitz, quoted Nietzsche: "He who has a reason to live endures almost any way". In the book Pursuit of Meaning, he teaches that meaning is found in work, love, and the attitude toward suffering. Practice: ask, what problem bothers me so much that I would like to solve? And serve a little bit in that direction this week.

licoes.r: Everything passes, the pain, the joy, the stages. To accept impermanence is to stop fighting the river.
licoes.a: In Buddhism, impermanence, anicca, is one of the three marks of existence. Heraclitus taught that one does not step twice into the same river, because the waters are different and so are you. She's not a cause for sadness. She's a cause for presence. Practice: Today, look at someone you love like it's the last time, and say something true.

licoes.r: Silence is where wisdom speaks loudest. He who speaks less hears more and makes fewer mistakes.
licoes.a: Blaise Pascal wrote, in Thoughts: all the unhappiness of men comes from one thing, not knowing how to be quiet in a room. The desert priests of the fourth century said, "Go, sit in your cell, and the cell will teach you everything". Practice: Ten minutes a day without screen, without music, and without conversation. It's annoying at first. Then it reveals.

licoes.r: Meditating is training attention. Sit down, breathe, and when your mind runs away, bring it back without a fight. That return is the exercise. Research shows benefits for stress and anxiety with regular exercise.
licoes.a: Inner reading: In Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, yoga is defined as the cessation of mind fluctuations. It's not stopping to think forcefully, it's stopping to identify with each wave. Practice: Start with five minutes a day. Tell me to lead and I'll conduct a short meditation.

licoes.r: Awakening is realizing that you are not every thought that passes through your mind. You're the one watching. The word Buddha means just awakening.
licoes.a: Common signs: more presence, less reactivity and more compassion. Jung wrote, in a letter from 1916, "He who looks outside dreams; he who looks within awakens". Beware: awakening doesn't make anyone superior; if it makes you feel superior, it's still your ego speaking. Practice: three times today, stop and ask, am I awake now?

licoes.r: Expanding consciousness is seeing more: more perspectives, more depth and more connection. The classic paths are meditation, study, nature and silence.
licoes.a: The poet William Blake wrote in 1790: If the doors of perception were purified, everything would appear to man as it is, infinite. Beware of shortcuts. Extreme substances and practices can be harmful. True expansion is gradual, and you keep your feet on the ground. Practice: Today, listen carefully to someone who thinks differently from you.

licoes.t: The Big Bang and the Age of the Universe
p: the big bang and the age of the universe
licoes.r: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old. The Big Bang wasn't an explosion at one point, but the expansion of all space from an extremely hot, dense state.
licoes.a: This is backed up by strong evidence: the cosmic microwave background radiation, the spacing of galaxies, and the amount of hydrogen and helium in the cosmos. What was before, if there was one before, no one knows. The priest and physicist Georges Lemaître proposed the idea of the primordial atom in 1927 and 1931. Practice: look at the dark sky tonight; some of that light went out before the Earth existed.

licoes.r: Dark matter is something invisible that has gravity. We know it exists because of the effects: galaxies spin too fast for the matter we can see.
licoes.a: It would make up about 27 percent of the universe, compared with about 5 percent of ordinary matter. What it is, no one knows: no dark matter particle has been detected to date. To know that something exists without knowing what it is: that is an honest mystery.

licoes.r: In 1998, it was discovered that the expansion of the universe is accelerating. The cause has been dubbed dark energy, about 68 percent of everything that exists.
licoes.a: The discovery won him the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics. But dark energy is a name for our ignorance: we don't yet know what it is, or whether it's constant in time.

licoes.r: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light escapes. The boundary without a return is called the event horizon.
licoes.a: In 2019, the Event Horizon telescope showed the first image of the shadow of a black hole, the star M87, 55 million light-years away. Stephen Hawking predicted that black holes emit weak radiation and can evaporate, but this has not yet been observed. What happens at the center, in the singularity, is unknown.

licoes.r: Einstein showed that time does not pass the same for everyone: it runs slower at high speeds and near large masses. That's measured, not imagined.
licoes.a: GPS satellites correct this effect every day; otherwise, they would be miles off course. Traveling into the future, in a way, is possible. For the past, there is no evidence. And what time really is remains one of the greatest mysteries of physics. Einstein wrote, in a 1955 letter to the family of his friend Michele Besso: For us convinced physicists, the distinction between past, present and future is only an illusi

licoes.r: Life on Earth emerged about 3.5 to 4 billion years ago. How chemistry became biology, called abiogenesis, we still don't know in detail.
licoes.a: There are strong hypotheses, like the world of RNA and hydrothermal vents on the seafloor, and experiments that form life molecules from simple chemistry. But no one has created life from scratch in a lab. The first step remains a mystery.

licoes.r: We already know of more than 5,000 planets outside the solar system, the exoplanets. Life outside the Earth, however, has not yet been found.
licoes.a: The Fermi paradox asks: If the universe is so big and ancient, where is everyone? Life's empty answers are rare until we've looked hard enough. There is no evidence of alien visitation. The search continues, and the question is legitimate.

licoes.r: Multiverse is the idea that our universe would be one among many. It comes up in some theories, like eternal inflation and the many-worlds interpretation of quantum physics.
licoes.a: Honesty: it's a hypothesis, it's not proven, and maybe it can't even be tested. There are physicists who defend it and others who say it's not even science. Keep the question open, don't rush to close it.

licoes.t: Why there is something rather than nothing
p: why there is something rather than nothing
licoes.r: Why is there something instead of nothing? Leibniz asked that question over three hundred years ago, and it remains unanswered.
licoes.a: Physics explains how the universe evolves, but not why it exists. Religions, philosophies and scientists offer different paths, and none are proof. In the face of such a question, the wisest thing to do is wonder. The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote in Tractatus: The mystic is not how the world is, but that it is.

licoes.r: Why does brain matter generate experience, red from red, pain from pain? Philosopher David Chalmers called this the hard problem of consciousness.
licoes.a: Neuroscience maps a lot of what the brain does, but it still doesn't explain why feeling exists. The odds range from materialism to panpsychism, and none have won. You're the mystery that wonders about itself. Practice: for a minute, don't pay attention to things, pay attention to the fact that you perceive things.

p: where do the atoms come from
licoes.r: The carbon in his body, the iron in his blood and the calcium in his bones were forged into stars. You are literally star dust.
licoes.a: Hydrogen and helium came from the Big Bang. The heaviest elements were born from fusion within stars, from supernovae and from collisions of neutron stars. Carl Sagan said, we are a way for the cosmos to know itself.

p: what is the size of the universe
licoes.r: The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across. And there could be a lot more beyond what we can see.
licoes.a: It's larger than 13.8 billion light-years because space kept expanding as light traveled. It is estimated that there are hundreds of billions to trillions of galaxies. Whether the entire universe is finite or infinite, no one knows. Pascal wrote: The eternal silence of these infinite spaces terrifies me. And again: by space the universe embraces me; by thought I embrace it.

licoes.r: The Sun is a star about 4.6 billion years old. At its core, nuclear fusion turns hydrogen into helium and releases the light that sustains life.
licoes.a: Light that leaves the surface of the sun takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach you. It should shine for another five billion years. Every morning, you receive an energy born in the heart of a star.

licoes.r: Gravitational waves are ripples in space-time itself. Einstein predicted them in 1916, and the LIGO observatory first detected them in 2015.
licoes.a: The signal came from the merger of two black holes over a billion light years away. The measured deformation was less than a thousandth of a proton. The discovery won the 2017 Nobel Prize: for the first time, we heard the universe.

licoes.r: How the universe will end, no one knows for sure. The most widely accepted scenario today is an eternal expansion into a dark cold, thermal death, trillions of trillions of years from now.
licoes.a: Other scenarios are the Big Rip, where everything tears, and the Big Crunch, where everything contracts. The answer depends on dark energy, which we still don't understand. None of this threatens you: these are unimaginable times.

p: we are one with the universe
licoes.r: A reflection, not a science: the same atoms that make up stars make up you. The universe isn't just out there; it's also thinking through you.
licoes.a: This is a contemplative bridge. Science shows the common origin of matter; the meaning you give to it is your choice. Look at the sky tonight and remember: you are part of what you observe.

licoes.r: Free will is one of the oldest questions: are we free or is everything already determined? Philosophy and neuroscience are still debating, and no one has the final answer.
licoes.a: Benjamin Libet's experiments in the 1980s measured brain activity before conscious decision-making, but their interpretation is much debated. Espinosa thought we think we're free because we don't know the causes that drive us. Inner reading: freedom may be knowing these causes. Practice: Today, before you react, count to three and choose.

licoes.r: Occult comes from the Latin occultus: hidden, reserved. In the old schools, certain teachings were given only to initiates, not because they were forbidden, but because they required preparation. Esoteric, from the Greek esoterikos, meaning from within.
licoes.a: Inside reading: the great secret of tradition was never a formula kept in a safe. What is hidden is what is revealed only to those who are transformed; it is not surrendered, it is conquered from within. That's why the insiders said the secret protects itself. Practice: pick one lesson and live it for seven days before looking for another.

licoes.r: In the Republic, book seven, Plato describes prisoners chained in a cave, who see only shadows projected on the wall and think that's reality. One of them gets free, climbs up, sees the fire, then the sun, and realizes he's been living in shadows.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the cave is the conditioned mind; the shadows are the inherited opinions; the sun is the idea of Good, the truth that illuminates everything. Plato says the climb hurts: the light dims, and the liberated one wants to return to the shadows. And when he comes back to free the others, he's ridiculed. Practice: Today, identify a shadow, something you accept just because everyone else does, and investigate

licoes.r: Mystery schools were initiation cults. The Eleusinian Mysteries in Greece celebrated Demeter and Persephone for about a thousand years, until the end of the fourth century. Pythagoras founded in Crotona, about 530 B.C., a community of study, number and silence.
licoes.a: What is known and what is not known: the initiates of Eleusis were sworn to secrecy, and the secrecy was kept so well that to this day we do not know what they saw. Cicero wrote that there they learned not only to live with joy but to die with a better hope. About Egypt, there are priests with reserved knowledge and the mysteries of Isis from Roman times, but the idea of great Egyptian initiatory schools is largely a

licoes.r: The Emerald Tablet is a short, enigmatic text, the basis of alchemy, attributed to Hermes Trismegistus. It is her phrase: what is below is like what is above, and what is above is like what is below, to perform the miracles of the one thing.
licoes.a: Fact: The earliest known versions are in Arabic, between the sixth and tenth centuries, and the Latin translation circulated in Europe from the 12th century onward. Even Isaac Newton made his own translation. Inner reading: the alchemists sought to transform metals; the mystics read this as the transformation of one's own being. Practice: Read the sentence out loud in the morning and look for an example of it in your

licoes.r: Alchemy was chemistry before chemistry: it sought to turn metals into gold and find the philosopher's stone. At the same time, it was a symbolic language of inner transformation.
licoes.a: Inside reading: The stages of the Work were nigredo, the blackening; albedo, the whitening; and rubedo, the reddening. Carl Jung, in his 1944 book Psychology and Alchemy, saw this as the process of individuation: facing the shadow, purifying and integrating. The motto solve et coagula, dissolve and coagulate, applies to the soul. Practice: write a pattern of yours that needs to be dissolved and a value that needs to

licoes.t: Kabbalah and the Tree of Life
p: kabbalah and the tree of life
licoes.r: Kabbalah is the Jewish mystical tradition. Its central book, the Zohar, appeared in Spain in the late thirteenth century, promulgated by Moses of León. The Tree of Life shows ten sefirot, the emanations through which the infinite, Ein Sof, manifests.
licoes.a: Inside reading: In the sixteenth century, in Safed, Isaac Luria taught tzimtzum, the contraction of God to make room for the world, and tikun olam, reparation: every righteous act raises back fallen sparks of light. The Tree is also a map of the human being, from the root, Malkuth, to the crown, Keter. Practice: do an act of reparation today, an apology, a helping hand, without telling anyone.

licoes.r: Gnosis, in Greek, is knowledge: not that of books, but the direct knowledge, by experience, of the divine. The Gnostics were Christian and pre-Christian movements of the first to third centuries, such as the Valentinians and the Setians.
licoes.a: In the myth of some Gnostic groups, the material world was made by a lesser and ignorant god, the demiurge, and each person holds a spark of the true God, which is awakened by gnosis. That's their myth, not a historical fact. The church fought them as heretics, and many texts did not return until 1945 at Nag Hammadi. In the Gospel of Thomas, Jesus says, if you bring to light what is in you, it will save you. Practice

licoes.r: The Rosicrucians emerged with three manifestos published in Germany: the Fama Fraternitatis of 1614, the Confessio of 1615, and The Chemical Brides of Christian Rosenkreuz of 1616. They spoke of a secret brotherhood of sages who would reform knowledge.
licoes.a: Fact: Most historians see Christian Rosenkreuz as an allegorical figure, and the theologian Johann Valentin Andreae assumed to have written The Chemical Bridal. There's no proof the original fraternity ever existed. Then modern orders emerged, such as AMORC, founded in the United States in 1915. Inner reading: the rose in the center of the cross is the soul that blossoms in the midst of matter and suffering. Practice

licoes.r: Modern Freemasonry was born out of the masons' guilds. The Grand Lodge of London was founded in 1717. It is a fraternity with rites and symbols: the square, the compass, the raw stone and the polished stone.
licoes.a: Symbolic reading: the square is rectitude in actions, the compass is the limit of desires, and the work of life is to polish the raw stone that is yourself. Fact: Theories that Freemasonry rules the world have no evidence. One of the biggest lies about her was the fraud of Leo Taxil, who invented satanic rituals and confessed to the fraud in 1897. Practice: Choose an edge of your character and work on it this week.

licoes.r: Sacred geometry is the spiritual reading of shapes. Some of it is real mathematics: the golden ratio, about 1.618; the Fibonacci sequence, which appears in the spirals of sunflowers and pines; and the five Platonic solids.
licoes.a: Separating the real from the mystical: the spiral of sunflowers follows the true golden ratio for growth efficiency. But many popular claims that the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa, or the human body exactly follow the golden number are exaggerated or false when measured. The mystical reading, that the order of forms reveals a mind in the universe, is belief, beautiful and respectable, but belief. The Pythagoreans, accordi

licoes.t: Vedanta, Maya and Tat Tvam Asi
p: vedanta, maya and tat tvam asi
licoes.r: Vedanta is the philosophy that originates from the Upanishads in India. In the Advaita school, systematized by Shankara around the eighth century, the deep self, the Atman, is the same as the absolute, the Brahman. Maya is the illusion that makes us see only the separate surface.
licoes.a: In the Chandogya Upanishad, the sage Uddalaka teaches his son Shvetaketu: Tat tvam asi, you are that. Brihadaranyaka teaches the way of neti neti, it's not this, it's not this: you are not the body, nor the thoughts, nor the roles. Maya doesn't mean that the world doesn't exist. She means that it's not what it seems. Practice: in front of every thing you think you are, say, I'm not just this.

licoes.r: The Tao Te Ching is attributed to Lao Tzu and was compiled in China around the fourth century BC. There are eighty-one short chapters on Tao, the way, and Te, the virtue. It opens like this: the Tao that can be said is not the eternal Tao.
licoes.a: Inner reading: Tao teaches by water, which is the softest and conquers the hardest. Wu wei is action without force, in harmony with the flow. In chapter thirty-three: he who knows others is wise; he who knows himself is enlightened. Practice: Today, in a conflict situation, do as the water does, don't push, bypass.

licoes.r: Sufism is the mystical dimension of Islam: the path of love and remembrance of God, dhikr. Its most famous poet is Rumi, of the thirteenth century, whose work, the Masnavi, opens with the reed flute mourning the separation from the reed bed.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the flute is the soul, cut off from its origin, that sings of longing. Sufis talk about dying before you die: letting the ego die so that the real you can live. The dervishes of the Mevlevi order rotate like the planets around the center. Beware: many of Rumi's quotes on the Internet are either false or overly adapted. Practice: slowly repeat a sacred word, or just peace, for five minutes with your bre

licoes.r: The pineal gland produces melatonin, the sleep hormone, which is regulated by light and dark. In spiritual traditions, it is associated with the third eye, the Ajna chakra, the inner vision. Descartes called it the chief seat of the soul.
licoes.a: Honesty: The connection between the pineal gland and spiritual powers is belief, not science. The popular idea that it makes DMT for vision is not proven in humans. And no fluoride calcifying the soul: that's an Internet myth. Inner reading: Jesus said, in Matthew six, the lamp of the body is the eye; if your eye is simple, your whole body will be lighted. The third eye is the attention that sees without judgment. Pr

licoes.r: Akashic records would be a kind of memory of the universe, where everything that happened would be recorded. The idea comes from Theosophy in the late nineteenth century and was popularized by Edgar Cayce. Akasha, in Sanskrit, means space or ether.
licoes.a: Honesty: It's a theosophical belief, without any scientific evidence. Don't trust people who charge a lot to read your records. Inner reading: What is true is that nothing you do disappears without leaving marks, on you and on others. Your life is a living record. Practice: Write a page in your journal today; it is your most reliable record.

licoes.r: You know yourself was inscribed in the temple of Apollo at Delphi, next to nothing in excess. Socrates made this phrase the center of philosophy and said in the Apology: a life without examination is not worth living.
licoes.a: Inner reading: this is the key that all mystery schools share. It's not about memorizing the personality, it's about going through it to what's underneath. St. Augustine wrote: "Do not go out, return to yourself; in the inner man dwells truth". Practice: Write down three beliefs about yourself today and ask where each came from.

licoes.r: Discernment is the ability to separate the true from the false, even within the spirit world. Be suspicious of anyone who sells secrets, charges for activations, promises shortcuts, or says he's the only one with the truth.
licoes.a: Paul wrote: "Prove all things; hold fast to what is fine". The Buddha, in the Kalama Sutta, taught not to accept something merely by tradition, authority or rumor, but by examining whether it leads to good. Carl Sagan said that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. Practice: Before accepting a teaching, ask yourself, who benefits from it, and what can I verify?

licoes.r: The Matrix is the mind control system: everything that thinks for you without you realizing it, planted fears, fabricated desires, inherited beliefs and authorities that can't be questioned. The religious matrix is one of the oldest, because it messes with what we hold most sacred. For centuries, fear, guilt, inquisitions and tithing in exchange have been used to govern consciences. Say more, Pandora's box or break the matrix.
licoes.a: The mechanism is always the same, whether in politics, in markets or in religion: first you create fear or guilt; then you sell the solution; finally you forbid the question. Psychiatrist Robert Lifton in 1961 called this thought reform, and Steven Hassan's BITE model describes the control of behavior, information, thought and emotion. The problem isn't sincere faith; it's who profits from fear. Practice: Today, look

licoes.r: The 1999 film The Matrix recounted old ideas. Plato, with the cave. Descartes, in his Meditations of 1641, imagined an evil genius capable of deceiving all the senses. And Jean Baudrillard, in Simulacrus and Simulation, 1981, said that we live among copies that no longer refer to anything real. His book is in the movie.
licoes.a: Inside reading: the phrase welcome to the desert of the real comes from Baudrillard. He himself said in 2004 that the film misunderstood him: for him there is no simple way out of a real world out there. The point is not to run away from a computer, it's to see that image, propaganda and opinion have taken the place of direct experience. Practice: spend an hour today experiencing something without taking a picture or

licoes.r: In Indian tradition, Maya is the veil that makes us take our appearance whole. It doesn't mean the world doesn't exist, it's that it's not what it seems at first glance. Behind the veil is the unity that the Upanishads call Brahman.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the veil is woven by ourselves, with names, labels, desires and fears. Arthur Schopenhauer, in the 19th century, brought the idea into European philosophy as the veil of Maya that separates beings. When the veil thins, compassion is born: you recognize yourself in the other. Practice: look at a stranger today and remember that he also wants to be happy and not suffer.

licoes.r: In 2003, philosopher Nick Bostrom published the argument that we might be living in a computer simulation. It's a philosophical argument, not a scientific discovery, and it's not proven.
licoes.a: No one has proof for or against it, and it may not even be possible to test. Inside reading: the question is old, Zhuangzi in China dreamed he was a butterfly and woke up not knowing if he was a man dreaming he was a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming he was a man. Practice: even if everything was a simulation, your values, your pain and your choices would still be real to you; live as if they mattered.

licoes.r: Ivan Pavlov showed that a dog learns to salivate by hearing a sound that used to come with food. That's conditioning: the mind associates without thinking. Humans are also conditioned by family, school, religion, and propaganda, especially in childhood.
licoes.a: A belief repeated before the age of seven is usually perceived as truth, not opinion. That's why so many people stand for ideas they never chose. Inner reading: conditioning is not your fault, but becoming aware of it is your responsibility. Practice: Write down three phrases you heard a lot as a child about money, God, and yourself, and ask yourself if you still agree with them.

licoes.r: Edward Bernays, Freud's nephew, founded modern public relations. In Propaganda, 1928, he wrote that the conscious and intelligent manipulation of the habits and opinions of the masses is an important element in democratic society. In 1988, Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky described, in The Making of Consent, how the media filters information.
licoes.a: Real example: In 1929, Bernays organized the Freedom Torch Parade, women smoking in public in New York City, to sell cigarettes to women as a symbol of freedom. Herman and Chomsky's five filters are: owner, advertiser, official sources, pressure against dissent, and a common enemy. This is not a secret conspiracy, it's a documented structure. Practice: on every news story today, ask, who paid, who profited, and who w

licoes.r: In 1971, economist Herbert Simon wrote that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. Today, apps compete for your attention, and algorithms learn what keeps you on the screen, often fear and anger, which hold you the most.
licoes.a: The mechanism is variable reward, studied by B. F. Skinner: Like a nickel-and-dime machine, you don't know when the next thing is coming, so you keep pulling. If the product is free, your attention is on the product. Practice: remove notifications from all non-person apps, and leave your cell phone out of your room tonight.

licoes.r: In 1955, analyst Victor Lebow wrote that the economy demands that we make consumption a way of life and that we seek spiritual satisfaction in shopping. Consumerism turns desires into needs and identity into product.
licoes.a: Inside reading: the ad almost never sells the thing; it sells a feeling, belonging, being loved, being safe. When the purchase comes, the feeling goes away, and the next desire is born. The Buddhists call this thirst tanha. Practice: Before you buy something you don't need, wait 48 hours and ask yourself, how do I want to feel about it?

licoes.r: In the 1950s, Solomon Asch showed that many people deny what they see in order to agree with the group. In 1963 Stanley Milgram showed that sixty-five percent of the participants shocked what they believed to be four hundred and fifty volts just because an authority ordered it. The shocks were fake, but the obedience was real.
licoes.a: Another powerful bias is confirmation bias: We look for what confirms what we already believe. These mechanisms work in any alternative group, church, party or movement. Practice: Today, look for the best argument against one of your beliefs, written by someone who thinks differently.

licoes.t: Fear as a Tool of Control
p: fear as a tool of control
licoes.r: Fear turns off slow thinking and turns on survival mode. Those who are afraid obey, buy and don't ask. That's why fear is the preferred tool of those who want to control.
licoes.a: In Nuremberg in 1946, Hermann Göring told the psychologist Gustave Gilbert that it is easy to drag the people along: just say they are under attack and accuse the pacifists of a lack of patriotism. The record is in the Nuremberg Diary. The same is true of religious, economic, or health fears when they are exaggerated to sell something. Practice: When faced with a frightening message that calls for urgent action, wait

licoes.r: Debt can become an invisible prison: the debtor works for interest and loses his freedom of choice. The book of Proverbs says: "The borrower is a slave to the lender".
licoes.a: Basic financial education, no investment advice: compound interest works for those who save and against those who owe. The revolving credit card in Brazil is among the most expensive interest rates in the world. Steps: List all debts, pay the higher-interest ones first, negotiate, and cut the easy credit. Practice: Write down all your installments today and add up how much of your income is already committed.

licoes.r: The ego is the voice that needs to be right, seen and defended. It's an identity program, made up of name, history, opinions and wounds. He's not an enemy. He's a servant who thinks he's a king.
licoes.a: Buddhism teaches anatta, the non-self: what you call the self is a process, not a fixed thing. Neuroscience observes something similar in a brain network connected to thinking about yourself, which is calmed down in meditation. Practice: Observe when you are easily offended or need to win an argument. There's the ego. Just noticing, he's already losing his strength.

licoes.t: How to Get Out of the Matrix
p: how to get out of the matrix
licoes.r: Leaving the Matrix isn't denying the world or falling for conspiracy theories, which is just another Matrix. It's about observing one's own mind, questioning the automatic and making conscious choices. The first gate is to notice when you're on autopilot.
licoes.a: In practice: one, turn off the noise, less news and screens; two, examine your inherited beliefs; three, learn to recognize the fear used to control; four, check sources; five, cultivate silence; six, live what you've discovered, with love. Gurdjieff called self-remembering the effort to be present as one acts. Practice: tell me to break the matrix, and I'll guide the journey in seven steps.

licoes.r: The Bavarian Illuminati really existed: a society founded on May 1, 1776 by Adam Weishaupt, and banned by the Bavarian government between 1784 and 1785. There's no evidence that they survived or that they control the world. Reptilians, flat earth and the myth that vaccines cause autism also have no evidence.
licoes.a: The mechanisms of power that are documented are no secret: concentration of wealth, lobbying, propaganda, campaign finance, debt. It's more useful to know them than to hunt shadows. Conspiracy theories tend to be as addictive as the Matrix itself: they give you an enemy, a sense of being chosen, and no one needs to prove anything. Historical fact: The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, the basis of much conspiracy, was

licoes.r: Spirituality is the living experience of the sacred. Institution is the human organization around it, with rules, hierarchy and money. The two can go together, but they're not the same thing. The problem isn't faith, it's who profits from fear.
licoes.a: Jesus drove out the merchants from the temple and said, in John four, that the hour was coming when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. A lot of institutions do real good, hospitals, schools, charities. The warning sign is when the institution puts itself in God's place. Practice: ask yourself, does my practice make me more free and loving, or more

licoes.r: Indulgence was the reduction of the penalty for sins in purgatory granted by the Church. In the early sixteenth century, it was sold en masse, also to finance St. Peter's Basilica. On October 31, 1517, Martin Luther published the 95 Theses against this trade, and the Reformation began.
licoes.a: The preacher Johann Tetzel is credited with the rhyme: When the coin in the box ticks, the soul in purgatory jumps. Luther replied in thesis 27 that this was a human doctrine. Fact: The Church itself, at the Council of Trent, banned the sellers of indulgences in 1562. Inside reading: forgiveness bought is fear managed. Practice: ask every spiritual promise, does it ask for my money or my transformation?

licoes.t: Religion in the Service of Power
p: religion in the service of power
licoes.r: Throughout history, religion has often been used to justify power, war, and colonization. Papal bulls of 1452 and 1493 authorized kings to take lands and enslave non-Christian peoples. Beginning in 1513, the Spanish read the Requerimiento to the natives, a requirement that they submit to the church and the king before attacking.
licoes.a: The other side is also true: Friar Bartolomé de las Casas denounced the massacres of the natives, and Quakers and pastors led the fight against slavery. Inner reading: whenever the sacred is used to dominate, it ceases to be sacred and becomes a tool. In 2023 the Vatican repudiated the doctrine of discovery. Practice: say the crimes of the church to see the historical archive with the sources.

licoes.r: Prosperity theology teaches that faith and giving bring wealth and health. It was born in the United States, in the Word of Faith movement of the twentieth century, with preachers like Kenneth Hagin and the seed of faith of Oral Roberts, and grew very much in Brazilian Neo-Pentecostalism. This is not true of every evangelical church: many reject it.
licoes.a: The mechanism: tithing becomes exchange, giving to receive, and one who does not prosper is guilty of having little faith. It exploits the believer's own desire. Facts: In Brazil, temples of any denomination have immunity from taxes by the Constitution, Article 150, paragraph six, letter b; and there is an evangelical parliamentary front in Congress. Paul wrote that each one should give as he has resolved in his hear

p: how do you know if a church
licoes.r: A manipulative group, religious or not, usually shows these signs: constant guilt and fear; money as proof of faith; a leader who cannot be questioned; isolation from outsiders; prohibition from asking or reading reviews; and a terrible fear of leaving. Steven Hassan put this together in the BITE model: control of behavior, information, thought and emotion.
licoes.a: How do you know? Ask yourself, can I disagree with the leader without being punished? Can I read criticism of the group? Can I leave without losing my family and friends? Where does the money go, and is there accountability? If the answer is no to several, it's a red flag. Robert Lifton, in 1961, described eight criteria of totalitarianism, such as control of the environment, loaded language, and doctrine above the p

licoes.r: The sacred texts did not fall ready from heaven in a single day: they were written, copied, assembled, and selected over the centuries by human communities. That is a historical fact, and it does not diminish anyone's spiritual worth.
licoes.a: Examples: the Council of Nicaea in 325 did NOT choose the books of the Bible, that is a myth; the canon was gradually formed from the second to the fifth century, and was fixed by the Catholic Church at Trent in 1546. There are lost gospels, the apocrypha, and many were rediscovered in Nag Hammadi, Egypt, in 1945. Practice: Read an entire Gospel at once, like a book, and notice what the text itself says.

licoes.t: The Kingdom of God Is Within You
p: the kingdom of god is within
the kingdom of god is within you
licoes.r: At Luke 17:21, Jesus says: The kingdom of God does not come with visible signs; the kingdom of God is within you. The Greek word entos can be translated as within or among you, and both readings exist. In the Gospel of Thomas, the third statement says: the kingdom is within you and outside of you.
licoes.a: Inside reading: if the Kingdom is inside, no institution owns the door. Meister Eckhart, a 14th-century Catholic mystic, spoke of the ground of the soul where God and the soul are one.
