St. Augustine said that God is more intimate than my innermost self. Practice: five minutes of silence with your hand on your chest, not asking for anything, just being.

licoes.t: Religious Matrix: Guilt, Fear, Anger and Greed
p: religious matrix guilt, fear, anger and greed
licoes.r: The religious matrix spins on four gears. Guilt: you're born in debt and you're never good enough. Fear: hell, curse, and punishment. Anger: an external enemy, us against them. Greed: give to receive, which exploits the desire of one's own faithful. Together, they form a self-feeding cycle.
licoes.a: The cycle: guilt creates the need for forgiveness; fear prevents questioning; anger toward outsiders keeps the group together; the promise of reward keeps giving. Hassan calls it emotional control in the BITE model. Spinoza, in the preface to his 1670 Treatise on Theology and Politics, taught that superstition springs from fear, is sustained by fear, and is fed by it. And Henri Tajfel showed in the 1970s that just di

licoes.r: Fear of hell works as control because infinite punishment gives infinite power to whoever claims to have the key; because it cannot be verified; and because it creates the problem and sells the solution. Fear turns off thought, and guilt closes the trap: control becomes automatic, from the inside out.
licoes.a: Psychology helps us understand: Kahneman and Tversky showed that fearing loss weighs more heavily than wishing for gain; and Terror Management Theory, based on Ernest Becker's 1973 book Death Denial, shows that fear of death causes us to cling tightly to the group's worldview. History: The Hebrew Sheol was the place of the dead, not of torture; Gehenna was the Valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem; the idea of hell develop

p: what s the conclusion of all this
qual a conclusao de tudo isso
licoes.r: The sum of history: Inquisitions with some three to five thousand executions in Spain and over a thousand and one hundred in Portugal; forty to sixty thousand killed in the witch hunt; some two hundred and sixteen thousand victims of clergy abuse in France alone since 1950; thousands of children killed in boarding schools and mothers' and babies' homes. The bottom line: more power, more authority that can't be questioned, more fear, equals abuse.
licoes.a: This formula is not unique to religion: atheist regimes of the 20th century, such as Stalin's, Mao's and the Khmer Rouge, political sects and gurus did the same. And the other side is also true: faith built hospitals, Quakers fought against slavery since 1688, and the Rev. Martin Luther King led the fight for civil rights. The right word for the mechanism: Robert Lifton, in 1961, called it thought reform and totalita

p: hermes trismegistus, commonly known as the hermes hermes
licoes.r: Hermes Trismegistus, the three times greater, is a legendary figure, the fusion of the Greek god Hermes with the Egyptian Thoth. There's no proof that he ever existed as a person. The texts attributed to him, the Corpus Hermeticum, were written in Greek in Roman Egypt around the second and third centuries.
licoes.a: In the Renaissance, Marsilio Ficino translated the Corpus in 1463 thinking it was older than Moses. In 1614, Isaac Casaubon showed by language that it was from the Christian era. Inner reading: Hermes is the messenger between the worlds, the mind that connects high and low. Practice: read the Emerald Tablet and think of a bridge between your inside and your outside.

licoes.r: Pythagoras of Samos lived in the sixth century B.C.E. and founded in Crotona, southern Italy, a community of study, dance, music, and discipline. He left nothing written; almost everything we know came from his disciples and much later authors.
licoes.a: The Pythagoreans taught that number is the essence of things and that the stars produce a harmony of the spheres. The theorem that bears his name was already known to the Babylonians. Inner reading: the order of the cosmos and the order of the soul correspond. Practice: end the day like the Pythagoreans, according to tradition, reviewing what you did, what you didn't do, and where you went wrong.

licoes.r: Heraclitus of Ephesus lived about 500 B.C. He taught that everything is changing, that opposites unite, and that there is a Logos, a reason that governs everything. Only fragments of his work remain.
licoes.a: Fragments known: one cannot step twice into the same river; the way up and down is one; the character of man is his destiny. He was called the Dark One because he spoke in riddles. Practice: today, when something changes against your will, say, the river is different, and so am I.

p: i just know i don t know anything
licoes.r: Socrates of Athens died in 399 B.C.E., condemned to drink hemlock for corrupting youth and failing to honor the city's gods. He wrote nothing; we know him as Plato and Xenophon.
licoes.a: His method was to ask until the person saw the contradictions of one's own certainties: the maiutic, the birth of ideas. In Apology, he says that a life without examination is not worth living. The phrase I only know that I know nothing is a popular summary; Plato writes that he claimed to be wise only because he knew that he did not know. Practice: pick one certainty and give it three why's.

licoes.r: Plato, a disciple of Socrates, founded the Academy of Athens about 387 B.C.E. He taught that the world we see is a shadow of a world of eternal Ideas, and that the soul remembers the truth.
licoes.a: The Allegory of the Cave in Book Seven of the Republic sums it all up. For Plato, philosophy is born of awe and is a preparation for death, that is, a detachment from what passes. Practice: Today, in front of something beautiful, ask yourself, what greater beauty is this reflection of?

licoes.r: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, which means awakened, lived in northern India around the fifth century B.C. He taught the Four Noble Truths: there is suffering; it has a cause, attachment; it can cease; and there is a path, the Noble Eightfold Path.
licoes.a: The middle way avoids both excessive pleasure and mortification. The Dhammapada begins like this: the mind precedes all things. And teach: hatred never ceases by hatred; only by love does it cease. Beware: many Buddha quotes on the Internet are false. Practice: Watch your breathing for ten minutes.

licoes.r: Lao-tse, the old master, is the sage to whom the Tao Te Ching is attributed. According to legend, he left China riding a buffalo and wrote the book at the request of a border guard. Historians do not know whether he existed as a person; the book seems to have been compiled in the fourth century before Christ.
licoes.a: The central teaching: to live in harmony with the Tao, with simplicity, humility and effortless action. Chapter sixty-four: the journey of a thousand leagues begins beneath your feet. Practice: Do something today that's slower than usual, with full concentration.

licoes.r: Most historians, believers and nonbelievers, agree that Jesus of Nazareth existed, was a Jewish preacher from Galilee, and was crucified in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate about 30 C.E. The center of his teaching is God's Kingdom and love for God and neighbor, even the enemy.
licoes.a: In the Sermon on the Mount, in Matthew five to seven: Blessed are the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart; pray in secret; do not lay up treasures on earth. He denounced those who laid heavy burdens on the shoulders of others and challenged the religious hypocrisy of his day. Practice: Choose a bliss and live it today.

licoes.r: Jalal ad-Din Rumi, Persian poet and Sufi master, lived from 1207 to 1273 in Konya, in modern-day Turkey. His encounter with the wandering mystic Shams of Tabriz turned him into a poet of divine love. His greatest work is the Masnavi.
licoes.a: The Masnavi opens with the reed flute that weeps the separation from the reedbed: the soul that yearns for its origin. His followers founded the Mevlevi order, the spinning dervishes. Beware: many of Rumi's phrases circulating on the Internet have been invented or heavily altered, and some erase their Islamic roots. Practice: Listen to a song in complete silence, with your eyes closed, as if it were a prayer.

licoes.r: Master Eckhart, a German Dominican friar, lived from about 1260 to 1328. He was one of the greatest Christian mystics. Some of his phrases were condemned by Pope John XXII in 1329, after his death.
licoes.a: He spoke of the depths of the soul, where God gives birth to the Son, and of detachment, the Gelassenheit, letting go. A real phrase from a sermon: The eye with which I see God is the same eye with which God sees me. Practice: For five minutes, stop asking and just stay.

licoes.r: Carl Gustav Jung, Swiss psychiatrist, lived from 1875 to 1961. He broke with Freud and created analytical psychology, with ideas like the collective unconscious, archetypes, shadow and individuation, the process of becoming whole.
licoes.a: Jung studied alchemy, gnosticism, myths and religions as maps of the soul. In a 1916 letter, he wrote: "He who looks outside dreams; he who looks within awakens". And in Alchemical Studies, no one becomes enlightened by imagining figures of light, but by making darkness conscious. Practice: Write down one dream a day for a week.

p: the truth and a land without roads
a verdade e uma terra sem caminhos
licoes.r: Jiddu Krishnamurti, an Indian, lived from 1895 to 1986. He was created by the Theosophical Society to be the new teacher of the world, but in 1929 he dissolved the order created for him and said: truth is a pathless land.
licoes.a: He refused to be a guru and taught nonjudgmental observation, freedom from all spiritual authority, including his own. A famous phrase attributed to him, that it is not a sign of health to be adapted to a sick society, has no confirmed source in his works. Practice: observe a thought without condemning or justifying it.

licoes.r: Ouroboros is the snake, or dragon, that bites its own tail. It appears in ancient Egypt, in a funerary text from the tomb of Tutankhamun, and later in Greek alchemical manuscripts.
licoes.a: It means the eternal cycle: the end that becomes the beginning, the unity of all. In alchemy, it accompanied the Greek phrase one is the whole. Jung saw in him the image of the process of self-transformation. Practice: Observe a cycle of yours that repeats itself, and ask what it wants to teach.

licoes.r: The Eye of Horus, the udjat, is an Egyptian amulet of protection, healing and wholeness. In the myth, Horus loses his eye fighting Seth, and the god Thoth restores it.
licoes.a: Not to be confused: The Eye of Providence, the eye within a triangle of rays, is a Christian symbol of the Trinity and divine watchfulness, appearing on the reverse of the one-dollar bill since 1935 and on the Great Seal of the United States since 1782. He's not a symbol of the Illuminati; that's myth. Practice: Remember today something wounded in you that has already been restored.

licoes.r: The Flower of Life is a pattern of equal circles that overlap in six-sided symmetry. It's an ancient geometric figure found in many cultures, and Leonardo da Vinci drew it in his notebooks.
licoes.a: Honesty: There are drawings of her in the temple of Osiris in Abydos, Egypt, but they're probably much more recent than the temple. The idea that it contains all the knowledge of the universe comes from New Age authors like Drunvalo Melchizedek in the 1990's; it's belief, not fact. The geometry itself is beautiful and real. Practice: draw it with a beat, slowly; it's a meditation.

licoes.r: The yin-yang, or taijitu, is the Chinese symbol of two complementary forces: yin, the dark, receptive, cold; yang, the light, active, warm. The design we know became popular from the Song dynasty, around the 11th century.
licoes.a: The essential point is the two dots: there is a little bit of yang in yin and a little bit of yin in yang. Nothing is pure; everything turns into its opposite. Practice: when you're at an extreme today, look for the seed of the opposite within him.

licoes.r: The Tree of Life appears in many cultures: in the Garden of Eden, in Genesis; as Yggdrasil, the Norse world tree; in Kabbalah, with the ten sefirot; and in cultures of Mesopotamia.
licoes.a: It connects three worlds: the roots in the subterranean, the trunk in the earth, the top in the sky. It's the axis of the world, where you go up and down in consciousness. In Revelation, the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. Practice: Put your feet on the ground barefoot for five minutes, feeling the roots.

licoes.r: The circumpoint, a circle with a point in the center, is one of the oldest symbols of the Sun. In Egypt it was the hieroglyph of Ra; in astronomy and alchemy it represents the Sun and gold.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the point is consciousness; the circle is the world it illuminates. The sun was honored as a symbol of the divine by Egyptians, Greeks, Incas and many others. Plato compared the idea of Good to the sun, which gives light to see and life to grow. Practice: At dawn, look at the light, never directly at the sun, and say thank you.

licoes.r: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC for Pharaoh Cheops. Archaeological evidence shows that it was made by organized Egyptian workers housed in villages near the site, not by slaves or extraterrestrials.
licoes.a: Findings such as Merer's diary, papyri more than four thousand five hundred years old, record the transportation of limestone blocks. Symbolic reading: the pyramid is the primordial mountain, the ascent of matter into the sky, the broad base and the unique apex. Practice: Think of your life as a pyramid: What base supports its highest point?

licoes.r: The lotus flower rises in the mud and blooms clean above the water. So in Hinduism and Buddhism, she is the symbol of purity and awakening in the midst of the world. In Egypt, the blue lotus symbolized the rebirth of the sun.
licoes.a: Fun fact: The lotus leaf repels water and dirt by a microstructure called the lotus effect, which has been studied by science. In the Bhagavad Gita, one who acts without attachment is likened to a lotus leaf that does not get wet. Practice: in the face of a harsh environment today, remember the lotus: to be there without staining.

licoes.r: The caduceus is the staff of Hermes, with two coiled snakes and wings on top. It's a symbol of the messenger, of trade and reconciliation of opposites.
licoes.a: Fact: The correct symbol of medicine is the staff of Asclepius, with a single snake and no wings. Confusion with the caduceus spread in the United States from 1902 when the U.S. Army adopted it. In esoteric reading, the two snakes are reminiscent of energies rising up the spine, as in yoga, to consciousness above. Practice: Breathe alternately through the nostrils for two minutes, balancing the two forces.

licoes.r: Mandala is Sanskrit for circle. In Hinduism and Buddhism it is a diagram of the cosmos and the spiritual path. Tibetan monks make sand mandalas for days and then undo them.
licoes.a: Jung observed that his patients drew mandalas spontaneously in phases of inner reorganization, and he saw them as symbols of the Self, the center of the whole. He himself drew one a day around 1918. Practice: Draw a circle and fill it out without planning, starting in the center.

licoes.r: For Jung, the shadow is the part of us that we don't accept and hide from ourselves: anger, envy, desires, but also rejected talents. What we don't look at, we project onto others.
licoes.a: Jung wrote, in Alchemical Studies: no one becomes enlightened by imagining figures of light, but by making darkness conscious. Integrating the shadow is not obeying it, it's recognizing it so it doesn't act in hiding. Practice: Write down the name of someone who irritates you the most and the quality that irritates him. Then ask, where does that live in me?

licoes.r: Archetypes, for Jung, are universal patterns of the psyche that appear in myths, dreams and religions around the world: the hero, the great mother, the wise old man, the cheater, the divine child.
licoes.a: Joseph Campbell, in The Hero of a Thousand Faces, 1949, showed the hero's journey repeated in many myths: the call, the refusal, the mentor, the crossing, the ordeal, the return with the elixir. It is an influential theory, not a law; critics point out that it simplifies the diversity of cultures. Practice: At what stage of the journey are you now?

licoes.r: Jung proposed that, in addition to the personal unconscious, there is a collective unconscious, common to all of humanity, from which archetypes would come. It's an influential hypothesis in psychology and religious studies, but it's not proven by experimental science.
licoes.a: Freud saw the unconscious above all as a repository of the repressed; Jung, also as a creative and religious source. Current neuroscience confirms that most mental processing takes place outside of consciousness, but this is different from Jungian theory. Practice: Before you go to sleep, ask your unconscious a question, and write down what comes up when you wake up.

licoes.r: Science knows that we dream mostly in REM sleep, several times a night, and that sleep helps consolidate memories and regulate emotions. Exactly why we dream is still unknown; there are several hypotheses.
licoes.a: Symbolic reading: Freud called the dream the via regia to the unconscious; Jung saw in it a compensation, showing what the consciousness ignores. For Jung, the dream speaks of the dreamer: each character can be a part of you. Be wary of dream dictionaries with fixed meanings; the symbol depends on your life. Practice: Leave a piece of paper by your bed and write down your dream before you get up.

licoes.r: Lucid dreaming is realizing you're dreaming inside the dream. It's been proven in the lab: in the 1970s, Keith Hearne, and in 1980, Stephen LaBerge, showed lucid dreamers sending combined signals with their eyes during REM sleep.
licoes.a: Techniques studied: reality tests during the day, asking am I dreaming?; the dream diary; and waking up in the morning and going back to sleep with the intention of realizing. Tibetan Buddhism has an ancient practice, dream yoga. Astral projection, as an actual exit from the body, has no scientific proof. Practice: five times today, look at your hands and ask, am I dreaming?

licoes.r: Synchronicity is the name Carl Jung gave to meaningful coincidences: seeing 11:11, thinking about someone and the person calling. He wrote about it in a 1952 essay with the physicist Wolfgang Pauli.
licoes.a: Science explains much of this by the confirmation bias: we notice what matches and forget the rest, and improbable coincidences are expected in a world of billions of events. Jung told the story of the golden beetle that hit the window while a patient was recounting a dream about a beetle. Practice: When you notice a sign, ask yourself, What good decision does it remind me to make? And use it wisely.

licoes.r: How it works: You're taught that you're born in debt and you're never good enough. Guilt becomes permanent, and forgiveness only comes through the institution. Example: sermons that remind you every week how unworthy you are, without ever announcing peace.
licoes.a: How to recognize: You feel guilty even for thinking, for resting, for having fun, and for relief only when you do what the group tells you to do. Lifton called it a requirement of purity and cult of confession. Note that the prophet Ezekiel already said, in chapter 18: the son shall not bear the guilt of the father.

licoes.r: How it works: Threatened with hell, curse or disgrace to anyone who disobeys, doubts, leaves or doesn't hurt. Example: If you leave the church, your family will be cursed.
licoes.a: How to recognize: the threat cannot be verified, but the fear is real and immediate; and the threat is the one that offers protection. It's the problem and solution pair. Say fear of hell to see the full story of that idea.

licoes.t: The Terror of the End Times
p: date of the end of the world
the terror of the end times
licoes.r: How it works: Announce that the end is near, sometimes with a date set, to create urgency: sell everything, donate everything, obey now. Historical example: The preacher William Miller dated Christ's return to 1844; it did not happen, and the episode became known as the Great Deception. Harold Camping set it for 2011.
licoes.a: How to recognize: urgency, date, request for money or break up with family. Jesus said, at Matthew 24:36, of that day and hour no one knows. And Deuteronomy, chapter eighteen, verse twenty-two, teaches that if what the prophet says does not come to pass, he has spoken presumptuously.

licoes.r: How it works: The donation is presented as an investment with a guaranteed return: sow to reap, make a pact, give what you don't have. Example: campaigns that promise healing, employment, or marriage in exchange for a high-value offer.
licoes.a: How to recognize: there is the promise of material return, public pressure, suggested values and blame for failure. Robert Cialdini described reciprocity as one of the principles of persuasion: whoever receives something feels obligated to give back, and here it reverses, you give expecting God to be obligated. But Paul wrote, at 2 Corinthians 9, that each one should give as he has resolved in his heart, not grudging

licoes.r: How it works: You're taught that you're only protected under the umbrella of the leader, and that disobeying him is disobeying God. Example: needing permission from the pastor to get married, change jobs or town.
licoes.a: How to recognize: The leader decides over his personal life, is not accountable, and treats any question as rebellion. In the BITE model, it's behavior control. Milgram showed how ordinary people obey authority even against their conscience.

p: don t touch the anointed one
you can t criticize the pastor
licoes.r: How it works: Psalm 105 is used, verse 15, "Touch not my anointed", to prohibit any criticism of the leader. For example, one who reports an abuse is accused of touching the anointed and threatened with punishment.
licoes.a: How to recognize: Read the context. In verses nine to fifteen, the psalm speaks of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, protected from foreign kings. In the story of David and Saul, in 1 Samuel 24, not touching is not physically hurting, and not forbidding speech. The prophet Nathan confronted King David about his sin, as recorded at 2 Samuel 12.

licoes.r: How it works: Doubt is called enemy attack, lack of faith, or rebellion. So one becomes a policeman of one's own mind. Example: that's the devil putting thoughts in your head.
licoes.a: How to recognize: You're afraid to think about certain questions. Lifton called sacred science, the doctrine that cannot be questioned, and loaded language, the clichés that enclose thought. In the BITE model, it's thought control.

p: they re friends of the church
don t mix with the world
nao se misture com o mundo
licoes.r: How it works: It teaches that the world outside is the devil's, that the unbelieving family is the enemy, and that only the group is safe. Example: discouraging friendships, studies, and programs outside the church.
licoes.a: How to recognize: your whole social life is inside the group, you only get information from it and you're afraid of people outside. Lifton called it environmental control, and the BITE model information control.

licoes.r: How it works: On arrival, the person receives undue attention, praise, and affection, and finally feels loved. Then that love becomes conditional on obedience. The term love bombing was used in the 1970's in connection with the Unification Church, and today it applies to cults and abusive relationships.
licoes.a: How to recognize: too much intensity too soon, too much haste for you to commit, and a sudden coldness when you disagree or fail. Cialdini described affection: we say yes to whom we like.

licoes.r: How it works: Anyone who errs or disagrees is exposed in front of everyone, removed from office or banned from participating. The fear of shame keeps the rest in line. Example: announcing from the pulpit the name of the one who is in discipline.
licoes.a: How to recognize: Punishment is public, disproportionate, and an example to others. Lifton called it a cult of confession: intimacy became an instrument of control.

p: i m nothing without the church
without the group, i m nothing
nao sou nada sem a igreja
sem o grupo nao sou nada
licoes.r: How it works: the group becomes your whole identity, your family, your agenda, your vocabulary and your value. Without it, you feel like a nobody. Example: every night of the week taken up with worship and homework.
licoes.a: How to recognize: You no longer know who is outside the group, and the thought of leaving causes panic. Lifton called it the doctrine above the person: actual experience is worth less than what the group says.

licoes.r: How it works: repetitive music, lights, fatigue, worship hours and collective shouting lead to a state of strong emotion, in which criticism drops. That's when the call comes, the money request or the decision. Example: the offer requested at the height of emotion.
licoes.a: How to recognize: emotion is not proof of truth. The same effects appear at concerts, rallies and cheerleaders. Cialdini shows the social proof: we do what we see others do. Emotion itself is beautiful; the problem is using it as leverage.

licoes.r: How it works: A promise of healing, a miracle, or prosperity in exchange for an offering, an anointing, a campaign, or payment. Documented example: In 1986, researcher James Randi revealed that televangelist Peter Popoff received, by electronic means, the information he claimed to come from God.
licoes.a: How to recognize: price, urgency, unverified testimony, and guilt by lack of faith when it doesn't work. The worst risk: abandoning medical treatment. Jesus said, in Matthew 10: freely you have received, freely give.

p: whoever gets out goes to hell
quem sai vai para o inferno
licoes.r: How it works: whoever leaves is called a deviant, a traitor, or a loser, and often loses family and friends all at once. The fear of that rejection keeps people for years in a place that already hurts them. Lifton called for the dispensation of existence: those who are outside have no value.
licoes.a: How to recognize: You stay not because of conviction, but because of fear of what they will say or do. Ask me, if I left, would anyone still love me?

licoes.t: The Inquisition in numbers and tortures
p: how many died in the inquisition
the inquisition in numbers and tortures
licoes.r: The figures that historical research supports: Spanish Inquisition, 1478 to 1834, about one hundred and fifty thousand tried and three to five thousand executed. Portuguese, from 1536 to 1821, about thirty to forty thousand trials, with one hundred and seventy-five burned in person, according to Henry Lea. Roman, after 1542, about one thousand two hundred and fifty death sentences, according to Andrea Del Col. Witch hunts in Europe, forty to sixty thousand executed, about eighty percent women, mostly by secular and local courts, Catholic and Protestant.
licoes.a: Torture was authorized by the bull Ad extirpanda of Pope Innocent IV in 1252. The best-known methods are the pole, or hook, which suspended the person by the wrists; the colt, a rope-bound easel; and the toca, water torture. The suffering went beyond the deaths: confiscation of property, the sambenito, clothes of shame worn in public, anonymous denunciations among neighbors and the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in

licoes.t: The Crusades and the Sack of Constantinople
p: the crusades and the sack of constantinople
licoes.r: The Crusades were wars called by popes, beginning in 1095, with the promise of forgiveness of sins to the combatants. In April 1204, the Fourth Crusade, which was to go to Jerusalem, plundered Constantinople, a Christian city, with massacres, rapes, and theft of relics, defying Pope Innocent III's prohibition.
licoes.a: In 1099 at the taking of Jerusalem, chroniclers of the time described a massacre of Muslims and Jews. Historians disagree about the exact numbers, and so they are not given here as certain. Pope John Paul II in 2001 apologized to Orthodox Christians for the sack of 1204.

licoes.r: On July 22, 1209, in the Albigensian Crusade against the Cathars of southern France, the city of Béziers was taken and the population massacred, including people taking refuge in the church. The pope's successor, Arnaud Amalric, wrote that almost twenty thousand were killed, his number probably exaggerated.
licoes.a: The phrase kill them all, God will recognize his own, is attributed to the legacy, but was not recorded until some thirty years later, by the monk Caesar of Heisterbach, and its authenticity is disputed. The crusade paved the way for the medieval Inquisition.

licoes.r: The Spanish Inquisition was established in 1478 and abolished in 1834. He persecuted mainly Jewish converts accused of maintaining the old faith, then Muslim converts and Protestants. It is estimated that some 150,000 were tried and 3,000 to 5,000 executed.
licoes.a: On March 31, 1492, the Decree of the Alhambra expelled Jews who would not convert; modern estimates range from forty to a hundred thousand expelled. Pope Sixtus IV himself, in 1482, denounced the greed of the inquisitors of Aragon, who were interested in the confiscated goods.

licoes.r: The Portuguese Inquisition ran from 1536 to 1821. According to Henry Lea, between 1540 and 1794 there were one thousand one hundred and seventy-five burned in person, six hundred and thirty-three in effigy, and more than twenty-nine thousand penitents. The file has more than thirty-five thousand cases.
licoes.a: Brazil never had its own court, but received visits, the first between 1591 and 1595, in Bahia and Pernambuco, and the prisoners were sent to Lisbon. The most persecuted were the new Christians, Jews forcibly converted in 1497. The playwright Antônio José da Silva, born in Rio de Janeiro, was guillotined and burned in Lisbon on October 19, 1739.

licoes.r: The philosopher and friar Giordano Bruno was burned alive by the Roman Inquisition on February 17, 1600, in Campo de' Fiori, Rome, after a seven-year trial. He advocated, among other ideas, an infinite universe with countless worlds.
licoes.a: Fact: He was condemned mainly for theological theses, such as denying the Trinity and the divinity of Christ, and not just for astronomy. Even so, he was killed for his ideas. Today there is a statue of him in the same place.

licoes.r: On June 22, 1633, the Roman Inquisition condemned Galileo on the strong suspicion of heresy for advocating that the earth revolves around the sun. He was forced to recant and spent the rest of his life under house arrest.
licoes.a: The phrase eppur si moves, and yet it moves, is probably a legend: it does not appear in records of the time. On October 31, 1992, Pope John Paul II publicly acknowledged the error of the Galilean judges.

licoes.r: Between about 1400 and 1775, Europe prosecuted about a hundred thousand people for witchcraft and executed forty to sixty thousand, about eighty percent women. The handbook Malleus Maleficarum, the Hammer of the Witches, from 1486, helped spread the panic.
licoes.a: Important fact: Most executions were carried out by local and secular courts, and there were witch hunts in both Catholic and Protestant regions. The Spanish and Roman Inquisitions, interestingly, were more skeptical and executed fewer witches. Germany concentrated most of the deaths.

licoes.r: At the beginning of the sixteenth century, indulgences, the remission of the penalties of purgatory, were sold en masse. Part of the money paid for St. Peter's Basilica and Archbishop Albert of Mainz's debts to the Fugger bankers.
licoes.a: In 1517, Luther protested with his 95 theses. The Council of Trent banned the sale of indulgences in 1562. Say indulgences and Luther for the full story.

licoes.t: The Doctrine of Discovery and Slavery
p: the doctrine of discovery and slavery
licoes.r: On June 18, 1452, Pope Nicholas V's bull Dum Diversas authorized the king of Portugal to subject Saracens and pagans to perpetual servitude. On May 4, 1493, the bull Inter caetera, by Alexander VI, gave Spain the newly discovered lands. These bills were used to justify colonization and slavery.
licoes.a: On March 30, 2023, the Vatican declared that the so-called doctrine of discovery is not part of Catholic teaching and that the bulls were used by colonial powers. The other side: religious men like Bartolomé de las Casas and, in Brazil, Father Antônio Vieira, denounced abuses against the natives, even though Vieira accepted African slavery.

licoes.r: From 1870 to 1997, about one hundred and fifty thousand indigenous children were taken from their families and put into boarding schools in Canada, most run by the Catholic Church and also by Protestant churches. More than 4,000 deaths have been documented, with estimates as high as 6,000.
licoes.a: In 2015, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission called the system cultural genocide: language ban, physical and sexual abuse, disease and starvation. In July 2022, in Maskwacis, Pope Francis apologized for the cooperation of many Catholics with this system.

licoes.r: In Ireland, from 1922 to 1996, Magdalene laundries, run by Catholic religious orders, confined women considered deviant, single mothers, orphans or poor to unpaid work. The most quoted estimate is about 30,000 women over the history of these institutions.
licoes.a: On 5 February 2013, the McAleese Report found significant involvement of the Irish State, and Prime Minister Enda Kenny issued an official apology. Religious orders have been criticized for not contributing to the repair fund.

licoes.t: Mother and baby homes in Ireland
p: mother and baby homes in ireland
licoes.r: The final report of the Irish Commission on Mother and Baby Homes, published on 12 January 2021, concluded that around nine thousand children died in eighteen institutions between 1922 and 1998, one in every seven born there. About fifty-six thousand women and fifty-seven thousand children passed through.
licoes.a: Many were run by Catholic orders. The case of Tuam, where remains of children were found in a sewer structure, shocked the country. The government issued a formal apology in 2021.

licoes.r: In May 2009, the Ryan Report of the Irish Commission to Investigate Child Abuse concluded that physical and emotional abuse was endemic in Catholic-run industrial and reformatory schools from 1936 onwards, and that sexual abuse was frequent in boys' institutions.
licoes.a: The report heard from over a thousand witnesses. It also showed that the State authorities failed to supervise. The names of many of the attackers have not been published because of a court case brought by the Christian Brothers.

licoes.t: Sexual Abuse and Cover-up in the United States
p: sexual abuse and cover-up in the united states
licoes.r: In January 2002, the Boston Globe's Spotlight team revealed that the Archdiocese of Boston was transferring priests accused of abuse from parish to parish rather than removing them. Cardinal Bernard Law resigned later that year. The story was made into the film Spotlight, which won the Oscar for Best Picture in 2016.
licoes.a: In August 2018, a Pennsylvania grand jury reported more than three hundred accused priests in six dioceses and more than a thousand victims identified over the course of seventy years with systematic cover-ups. These figures refer to documented charges, not all of which went to trial, because many cases were already prescribed.

licoes.r: In October 2021, the French independent commission CIASE, chaired by Jean-Marc Sauvé, estimated about two hundred and sixteen thousand victims of sexual abuse by clergy and religious in France since 1950, and about three hundred and thirty thousand including lay people who worked for the Church.
licoes.a: These are estimates made by statistical surveys with the population, not counting cases. The report spoke of the Church's deep and sometimes cruel indifference to victims for decades. The French bishops acknowledged institutional responsibility in November 2021.

licoes.t: Ambrosian Bank and the Vatican Bank
p: ambrosian bank and the vatican bank
licoes.r: In 1982, Italy's Banco Ambrosiano collapsed with a hole of about 1.3 billion dollars. The Vatican Bank, the IOR, headed by Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, was its main shareholder. The president of the Ambrosiano, Roberto Calvi, was found hanged under Blackfriars Bridge in London in June 1982.
licoes.a: In 1984 the Vatican paid out about $244 million to creditors, acknowledging moral involvement, without admitting guilt. Calvi's death, first treated as suicide, was later ruled a homicide by Italian justice, but the defendants were acquitted in 2007.

p: stolen children in franco s spain
licoes.r: During Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from imprisoned, poor or unmarried mothers and given to other families, often with the participation of nuns, priests and doctors. Judge Baltasar Garzón estimated that some 30,000 children were in the custody of the regime between 1944 and 1954.
licoes.a: Larger numbers, such as three hundred thousand, are disputed and not supported by recent research. There were investigations and trials, but few convictions, partly by prescription; the first defendant brought to trial, a doctor, had the crimes proven but was acquitted by prescription in 2018.

p: the church has asked for forfeiture
licoes.r: On March 12, 2000, Pope John Paul II celebrated the Day of Atonement, asking forgiveness for the sins of the children of the Church: intolerance and violence in the service of truth, divisions among Christians, the treatment of Jews, women and indigenous peoples.
licoes.a: He also apologized on other occasions: to Galileo in 1992; to the Orthodox for the sack of Constantinople in 2001. Pope Francis has apologized to Canada's indigenous people in 2022 and to the victims of abuse. The Church itself acknowledges that these events took place.

p: about the jews and their lies
sobre os judeus e suas mentiras
licoes.r: In 1543, Martin Luther published On the Jews and Their Lies, in which he called for Jewish synagogues and schools to be burned, houses destroyed, and books confiscated. At the beginning of his career he had been more tolerant.
licoes.a: Centuries later, Nazi propagandists used that text. In 1994 the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America publicly repudiated these writings, and other Lutheran churches followed suit.

licoes.r: On October 27, 1553, the physician and theologian Michael Servetus was burned alive in Champel, Geneva, for denying the Trinity. John Calvin helped prosecute him; he asked that he be beheaded rather than burned, but he supported the conviction.
licoes.a: Servetus was also wanted by the Catholic Inquisition: he was persecuted on both sides. In 1903, Protestants in Geneva erected an expiatory monument at the site, acknowledging the mistake.

licoes.r: In 1692 and 1693, in the Puritan colony of Massachusetts, more than two hundred people were accused of witchcraft in Salem. Nineteen were hanged, Giles Corey was crushed to death under stones for refusing to testify, and at least five died in prison.
licoes.a: The charges came from girls with seizures attributed to witchcraft, and the court accepted spectral evidence, visions and dreams. In 1697, the colony went on a fast for the mistake, and one of the judges, Samuel Sewall, publicly apologized. In 1711, there were reparations.

licoes.t: The Southern Baptist Convention and Slavery
p: the southern baptist convention and slavery
licoes.r: The Southern Baptist Convention, the largest Protestant denomination in the United States, was founded in 1845 after Northern Baptists refused to appoint slave-owning missionaries. It was therefore born in defense of the slaves.
licoes.a: In 1995, the Convention itself passed a resolution apologizing for slavery and support for racism. The other side: many Christians, like the Quakers since 1688, were voices for abolition, and black churches were the heart of the civil rights movement.

licoes.t: Abuses at the Southern Baptist Convention
p: abuses at the southern baptist convention
licoes.r: In February 2019, the Houston Chronicle and San Antonio Express-News newspapers revealed about three hundred and eighty leaders and volunteers of Southern Baptist churches accused of sexual abuse since 1998, with more than seven hundred victims.
licoes.a: On May 22, 2022, Guidepost Solutions' independent report showed that for nearly two decades, members of the Convention's Executive Committee ignored and discouraged victims from avoiding prosecution, and that one official kept a secret list of hundreds of defendants.

licoes.r: On November 18, 1978, in Guyana, nine hundred and eighteen people died in connection with Pastor Jim Jones' People's Temple, most of them poisoned with cyanide, including more than three hundred children. Earlier, a U.S. congressman, Leo Ryan, and four other people were shot dead on the runway.
licoes.a: The People's Temple was affiliated with the Disciples of Christ, a Protestant denomination. Jones used many techniques of the BITE model: total isolation, confessions, death trials, fear of external enemies and a leader who could not be questioned.

licoes.r: In 1989, American television evangelist Jim Bakker was convicted of twenty-four counts of fraud for selling more vague lifetime memberships in his religious park than there were, and for using the money for personal luxury. He received a sentence of forty-five years, reduced to eight, and was paroled in 1994.
licoes.a: In 2020, Bakker was sued in the state of Missouri for selling a colloidal silver product as a Covid cure; the case ended in a settlement, with refunds to buyers.

licoes.r: In 1986 researcher James Randi demonstrated that televangelist Peter Popoff received by e-mail from his own wife the names and diseases he said were revealed by God. In 1988, preacher Jimmy Swaggart, who had condemned other pastors, tearfully confessed to a sex scandal and was excommunicated by his denomination.
licoes.a: Popoff continues to sell miracle products on television. The pattern in these cases: spectacle, promise of a miracle, request for money and no accountability.

licoes.r: In Brazil, pastor and former federal deputy Flordelis dos Santos de Souza was sentenced by a jury on November 13, 2022, to fifty years and twenty-eight days in prison as the mastermind of the murder of her husband, pastor Anderson do Carmo, who was shot dead in 2019 in Niterói. Sons and others involved were also convicted.
licoes.a: She had her mandate overturned by the House in August 2021. The case shows how a public religious image can hide violence inside the home. It's a crime of people, not of the evangelical faith.

licoes.r: A portrait of Brazil today, with only verified facts. According to the IBGE 2022 Census, released in 2025, 56.7 percent of Brazilians declare themselves Catholics, 26.9 percent evangelicals and 9.3 percent without religion. The vast majority of communities are serious and welcoming. The problem arises where the usual formula comes together: power, more authority that cannot be questioned, more fear.
licoes.a: In this part of Pandora's Box are: tithing and campaigning, anointed objects and promised cures, mental illness treated as demonic, pressure on women, pulpit politics, misinformation, faith in television, debt forgiveness, and condemned crimes. Rule: accused is not convicted; here each case says exactly where you stand. Say themes from Pandora's box to see the list.

p: donate the house to the church
doar a casa para a igreja
licoes.r: Today, the request for bids also arrives via PIX, QR code on screen and live broadcasts. Some campaigns call for high values or goods with a promise of blessing, such as the Holy Fire of the Universal Church. In March 2022, according to the Legal Counsel, the Court ordered Universal to return two hundred and four thousand reais donated by an ex-client; in other cases, the donors lost.
licoes.a: The mechanism is tithing as exchange: give what you don't have for God to act. A donation made under emotional pressure at the height of a cult can be challenged in court when there's coercion, but it's not always recoverable. Giving out of gratitude is free; giving out of fear or promise of return is business.

licoes.t: Articles of ointment and dressings for sale
p: articles of ointment and dressings for sale
licoes.r: Water, oil, salt, scarves, and seeds are offered as bearers of blessing or healing. In August 2020, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office filed a public civil action against Pastor Valdemiro Santiago and the Worldwide Church of the Power of God for offering bean seeds, from a hundred to a thousand reais, with the promise of a cure for Covid; in October, a federal judge ordered the Ministry of Health to report that the bean has no proven efficacy.
licoes.a: Accuracy: In April 2022, according to the UOL, the São Paulo Public Prosecutor's Office requested the closure of the criminal investigation, stating that one of the videos that gave rise to the complaint had fraudulent editing. In other words: there was action and decision on health information, but no criminal conviction. This shows the double caution: to distrust the promise of a paid miracle, and also to check the

licoes.r: Depression is a disease recognized by the World Health Organization, with treatment. Saying that it's just a demon, a sin, or a lack of faith can delay seeking help and increase the guilt of those already suffering.
licoes.a: What Brazilian research shows is balanced: studies reviewed in the Journal of Clinical Psychiatry indicate that religiosity can protect mental health with support, meaning, and community. The damage happens when faith is used against treatment. Many pastors and priests today refer the faithful to a psychologist and psychiatrist, and that is the wise course.

p: pastor said to forgive her husband
woman picks up and the church
licoes.r: Brazilian surveys of evangelical women who experienced domestic violence, published in psychology journals in 2021 and 2025, show that certain readings about submission, obedience, and preserving marriage at all costs helped maintain violent relationships and delay reporting.
licoes.a: The same studies show the paradox: faith has also been a source of strength for many to break out of the cycle. A survey of a shelter in São Paulo concluded that the problem is not religion itself but the patriarchal way in which it is taught in some churches, functioning as a means of controlling women.

licoes.r: The election law, Law 9,504 of 1997, Article 37, prohibits election propaganda inside temples of any religion. In August 2020, the Higher Electoral Court decided not to create its own category of abuse of religious power, but recalled that propaganda in temples and church donations are already prohibited. In 2022, the newspaper O Globo reported campaigns in churches that led worshippers to react and even change churches.
licoes.a: The other side: State reports in 2022 showed that many evangelical women listen to the pastor, but decide the vote by their own reflection. Faith and citizenship can go hand-in-hand; abuse is turning spiritual authority into electoral corral.

licoes.r: In the 2022 elections, UFRJ's NetLab lab, with Casa Galilea, monitored seventy-five evangelical YouTube channels, as well as pages and profiles, and found narratives of spiritual warfare and election fraud among the most engaging. BBC Brazil showed that fake news about an alleged persecution of evangelicals reached millions.
licoes.a: The mechanism is that of attention economy: the algorithm delivers more than it captures, and fear and outrage capture a lot. Thus, apocalyptic and common enemy content spreads more than messages of peace.

licoes.r: In 2015, according to Ancine, religious programs accounted for 21.1 percent of monitored public TV programming. On RedeTV, they were 43 percent of the grid, much of it in hours sold, or leased, to churches. Today, the struggle also happens in networks, with influential pastors and prosperity coaching.
licoes.a: Fact: TV concessions are public, and the sale of time to third parties is a long-standing topic of debate and lawsuits. Reading: Faith has also become an audience market, and audience is measured in donations.

licoes.t: Immunity and Forgiveness of Churches' Debts
p: immunity and forgiveness of churches debts
licoes.r: The temples have immunity from taxes by the Constitution, Article 150, but it does not reach the contributions, like the CSLL and the social security. On March 17, 2021, Congress overrode a veto and excluded churches from the CSLL, nullifying past authorizations; the House voted 439 to 19 and the Senate, 73 to 1. The government has estimated renunciation of about 1.4 billion reais in four years.
licoes.a: According to the State, the Revenue had identified temples' maneuvers to distribute profits and remunerate pastors according to the number of faithful without paying these tributes; and the proposal was made by a deputy son of a church founder with debts to the Union. That was legal, voted and public; the question is ethical.

licoes.r: In January 2007, the founders of the Renascer em Cristo church, Estevam and Sônia Hernandes, were arrested at Miami airport with about 56,000 dollars in undeclared cash, part of it hidden inside a Bible. They pleaded guilty and in August 2007 were sentenced in the United States to one hundred and forty days in prison, house arrest, and a fine.
licoes.a: This is a conviction case, so get in here. Other cases of religious leaders being investigated for embezzlement or money laundering in Brazil were left out when there was no verifiable official conviction or denunciation.

licoes.r: The medium João Teixeira de Faria, the John of God, who attended thousands of people in a nursing home in Abadiânia, Goiás, was denounced for sexual crimes against sixty-six victims. As of September 2023, according to the Goiás Court of Justice, he has been convicted in the first instance of fifty-six of them, with sentences totaling four hundred and eighty-nine years and four months. There are pending resources.
licoes.a: Victims reported that the abuse happened during supposed spiritual treatments, using the authority of a healer. He does not represent spiritism, nor the serious mediums, who, as Kardec taught, do not charge. The case began to fall apart in 2018, when women had the courage to speak on television.

p: sexual abuse in the church in brazil
licoes.r: There are recent cases with convictions. In November 2024, according to G1, a pastor from Guaraí, Tocantins, was sentenced to more than thirteen years in prison for raping and abusing ten teenagers; he used an alleged anointing ritual. In April 2024, another pastor from Tocantins was sentenced to nine years for raping a teenage girl inside the church.
licoes.a: The pattern is the same as seen in the world: spiritual authority creates trust and silence, and the institution sometimes protects the leader. For the sake of truth, here only come cases of conviction reported by a reliable source; this does not mean that they are the only ones, nor that every leadership is suspect.

licoes.r: Children take words literally. Repeatedly hearing about hell, demons, and the end of the world can generate lasting fear. Psychologist Marlene Winell called religious trauma syndrome the combination of anxiety, nightmares, and guilt that some adults report after a fundamentalist upbringing. It's not an official diagnosis, it's a description.
licoes.a: Teaching family values and faith is a parent's right. The difference is in the method: love and meaning form; terror and threat wound. Many people carry this fear with them even after they change their beliefs, and it can be treated.

licoes.r: Some churches use, consciously or unconsciously, techniques that the psychology of persuasion describes: repetitive music, light, fatigue, collective catharsis, ever-successful testimonies, and multi-week chains, in which one small commitment leads to another larger one.
licoes.a: Robert Cialdini called this commitment and consistency: after saying a small yes, we tend to stay consistent with it. Add in the social proof, everybody's giving, and the scarcity, the opportunity is just today. The same techniques appear in sales and politics. Emotion is not a lie, but it's not proof.

licoes.t: How the Old Testament was Written
p: how the old testament was written
licoes.r: The Old Testament, the Hebrew Bible, was written, compiled, and edited over a period of nearly a thousand years, from about 1000 to 150 B.C.E., by many hands. Tradition ascribes the Torah to Moses, but historical research sees in it various sources and layers of editing.
licoes.a: In the 19th century, Julius Wellhausen formulated the documentary hypothesis: four sources, called J, E, D and P, combined over time. Many scholars today prefer patterns of fragments and supplements, but almost all agree that the Torah took its final form around the time of the Babylonian exile and later, in the sixth and fifth centuries before Christ. The book of Daniel, for example, is generally dated about 164 B.C

licoes.t: How the New Testament was Written
p: how the new testament was written
licoes.r: The earliest texts of the New Testament are the letters of Paul, about A.D. 50 to 60. The Gospels came later: Mark about 70 C.E., Matthew and Luke about 80 to 90 C.E., and John about 90 to 110 C.E. They circulated anonymously; the titles according to Matthew, according to Mark, were added in the second century.
licoes.a: Of the thirteen letters attributed to Paul, scholars consider seven to be certainly his: Romans, first and second Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, first Thessalonians, and Philemon. Others, such as the letters to Timothy and Titus, are viewed by most as pseudepigrapha, written later in his name, a common practice in antiquity. Practical: Read the entire Gospel of Mark, the oldest, at once.

licoes.t: Choosing the Books of the Bible
p: how did they choose the books
the apocryphal books of the old testament
choosing the books of the bible
licoes.r: No one picked everything at once. Around 140 C.E., Marcion proposed a list of his own, with only Luke and ten of Paul's letters, and this forced a reaction. About 180 C.E., Irenaeus defended the four Gospels. In 367, Athanasius of Alexandria listed in an Easter letter the twenty-seven books of the present New Testament. Regional councils in Rome in 382, Hippo in 393, and Carthage in 397 confirmed similar lists.
licoes.a: The list was not definitively fixed for Catholics until the Council of Trent on April 8, 1546, in response to the Reformation. Luther, in his 1534 Bible, singled out the deuterocanonical books, such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Baruch, and the Maccabees, as good to read but not equal to Scripture. That is why the Catholic Bible has seventy-three books and the evangelical sixty-six. Luther even called the

licoes.r: Constantine legalized Christianity with the Edict of Milan in 313 but did not make it the official religion; this came with Theodosius in the Edict of Thessalonica in 380. He convened the Council of Nicaea in 325, which did NOT choose the books of the Bible; that is the myth popularized by the 2003 book The Da Vinci Code.
licoes.a: Less well-known facts: His coins bore the Unconquered Sun until about 325; in 321 he decreed the day of the Sun, Sunday, as a day of rest; in 326 he had his own son, Crispus, executed, and his wife Fausta died the same year in suspicious circumstances; about 331 he commissioned Eusebius of Caesarea to send fifty copies of the Scriptures to the churches of Constantinople; and he was baptized on his deathbed in 337 by

licoes.r: The Council of Nicaea, in 325, gathered at least two hundred bishops, tradition says three hundred and eighteen, summoned by Constantine. He did NOT choose the books of the Bible. It dealt with three topics: the dispute with the priest Arius, who said that the Son was created and not eternal like the Father; the date of Easter; and norms for the clergy.
licoes.a: The council decided that the Son is homoousios, of the same substance as the Father, and approved the first Nicene Creed. Arius was exiled. Another common myth: That at Nicaea it was voted on whether Jesus was divine; the discussion was not whether he was divine but how. The Arian dispute continued for decades, and Constantine himself later favored Arian bishops.

licoes.t: The Lost Gospels and Nag Hammadi
p: the lost gospels and nag hammadi
licoes.r: In December 1945, near Nag Hammadi, Egypt, peasants found a jar with twelve papyrus codices and part of a thirteenth one, with fifty-two Coptic texts, copied in the fourth century. Among them is the complete Gospel of Thomas, with one hundred and fourteen sayings of Jesus.
licoes.a: Other non-canon texts have also appeared: the Gospel of Mary, in a codex purchased in 1896, and the Gospel of Judas, from the Tchacos Codex, published by National Geographic in April 2006, in which Judas appears as the disciple who understood Jesus. Many of these texts are Gnostic and post-canon gospels, but they show how diverse early Christianity was. In the seventy words of Thomas, if you bring to light what is in

licoes.r: The Dead Sea Scrolls were found beginning in late 1946 and 1947 by a Bedouin shepherd in the caves of Qumran, and by 1956 the remains of some nine hundred and eighty-one manuscripts, from eleven caves, written between the third century B.C. and the first century A.D., had emerged.
licoes.a: They contain the oldest known manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible, such as the Great Scroll of Isaiah, which is nearly complete and about a thousand years older than the manuscripts used up to that time. They show that the text was well preserved in many books, but also that different versions circulated. Many associate them with the Essenes, but this is debatable.

p: the bible has been tampered with
licoes.r: There are about five thousand eight hundred Greek manuscripts of the New Testament, and none of them are the original. They have many variations, mostly minor, in spelling and word order. But some are large: the episode of the adulterous woman, at John 7:53 to 8:11, and the long ending of Mark, 16:9 to 20, are not in the oldest manuscripts.
licoes.a: The Joanine Comma at 1 John 5:7, the phrase about the three witnesses in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, does not appear in ancient Greek manuscripts; Erasmus included it in the third edition of his Greek New Testament in 1522, and it entered many Bibles. Scholar Bart Ehrman popularized this in his book What Did Jesus Say? Misquoting Jesus, from 2005. Modern Bibles often mark these passages with fo

licoes.r: You come from a 2,000-year tradition of saints, mystics and martyrs. Nothing here asks you to abandon your faith. The invitation is to live the faith with an awakened conscience, as the Church itself teaches. I've saved his path; I'll add a key to it when we talk about the Matrix, church, Bible or Pandora's box.
licoes.a: Keys to awakening: The Catechism, in paragraphs 1776 to 1778, calls consciousness man's most secret and sacred core, where he is alone with God. Cardinal Newman, in 1875, wrote that if he had to toast, he would toast conscience first and the pope afterwards. St. Augustine: Don't go outside, go back inside yourself; in the inner man dwells truth. Matthew 23:9: Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your F

licoes.t: Who instigated David - God or Satan?
p: who instigated david - god or satan
licoes.r: 2 Samuel 24:1 says that the anger of the Lord was kindled and the Lord moved David to number Israel. 1 Chronicles 21:1, recounting the same event, says: Satan rose up against Israel and incited David to number Israel. Apologists' Answer: God allowed Satan to act, so each scripture highlights one side of the same action.
licoes.a: What research says: Chronicles was written centuries after Samuel, after the Babylonian exile, when the figure of an adversary, Satan, was gaining strength in Jewish thought. The chronicler seems to have avoided attributing to God an act that led to a plague. It's a rare example of seeing theology change within the Bible itself. Inner reading: Our idea of God grows over time, and the Bible records that growth.

licoes.r: 1 Samuel 17:50 says that David defeated the Philistine with a sling and a stone. 2 Samuel 21:19 says: "El-hanan the son of Jaare-orim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite. Apologists' answer: There was a copying error in 2 Samuel, and Chronicles preserves the correct reading; so some translations add Goliath's brother in 2 Samuel.
licoes.a: What the research says: Many scholars think otherwise, that the earliest tradition attributed the victory to El-hanan, a warrior of David, and that fame later passed to the king, as with national heroes. Chronicles, later, would have harmonized. Note that in the Almeida quoted here, 2 Samuel 21:19 does not use the word brother. Inner reading: hero stories grow; this applies to all peoples.

licoes.r: In the text, the one who acts is Satan, but with God's permission. Job 1:12: the Lord said to Satan, all that he has is in your power; only do not lay a hand on him. At 1:18-19, a strong wind collapses the house and kills Job's sons and daughters. And Job answers, in 1:21: The Lord hath given, and the Lord hath taken away. The apologists' answer: the book does not explain suffering, it shows that faith can cross it, and in the end God answers Job from the whirlwind.
licoes.a: What the research says: Job is a work of wisdom, probably a poetic parable, not a chronicle. Its center is a protest: Job questions God for dozens of chapters, and at the end, in Job 42:7, God says to his accusing friends: You have not spoken about me what is upright, as my servant Job has. Inside reading: The oldest book on suffering defends the right to complain to God, and condemns religious who blame the victim.

licoes.r: Narrated as done by humans. After the crime of Gibeah, the tribes attack Benjamin; in Judges 20:28, they consult the Lord, who answers, "Come up". But what follows is the decision of the assembly: at 20:46-48, they kill men and animals and burn the cities; at 21:10-12, they have all in Jabesh-gilead killed, sparing four hundred virgins; and at 21:20-23, they have the Benjamites ambush and take away the dancing girls of Shiloh. Apologists' response: The book ends by showing, on purpose, how far a people without law and without king can go.
licoes.a: What the research says: Scholars read the end of Judges as a propaganda for monarchy: Without a king, everything would be chaos. To repair one massacre, the people commit another, and to restore women, they authorize a kidnapping. Honesty: The first battle has divine approval in the text; the extermination of Jabesh and the abduction of Shiloh are human decisions, and the text does not say that God commanded them. In

At 12:9, the prophet Nathan accuses: Uriah the Hittite you have killed with the sword, and his wife you have taken. Apologists' answer: The Bible does not hide the sin of its heroes, and Psalm 51 shows David's repentance.

Nathan is a rare role model: a religious man who confronts power and says, that man is you, at 12:7. Inside reading: The anointed David also erred, and the prophet did not keep quiet. Apologists' Answer: Bethlehem was small, perhaps twenty children, which would explain why historians of the time did not record the fact, and Herod even killed the children.
licoes.a: What the research says: The historian Flavius Josephus records many atrocities of Herod, but not this one, which is recorded only by Matthew. At Nicaea, in 325, which he convened, the question was whether the Son was of the same substance as the Father; the Holy Spirit was barely discussed. licoes.a: What Constantine really did: he legalized Christianity in 313, convened and pressured the Council of Nicaea to end the dispute that divided the empire, and exiled those who did not sign. But later he changed sides: he called Arius back, exiled Athanasius, the greatest defender of Nicaea, in 335, and was baptized on his deathbed, in 337, by Eusebius of Nicomedia, an Arian bishop. licoes.r: Triads of gods exist in many cultures, and that is real. In Egypt, Osiris, Isis and Horus form a family: father, mother and son. But the idea that the Christian Trinity is a direct copy of one of them is not accepted by most historians. Pagan triads are almost always three different gods; the Trinity says one God in three persons, and it was born among Jews who swore there was only one God.

licoes.r: This is the so-called problem of hell, debated for centuries by philosophers, including Christians. The argument: a human life is short and limited, so no mistake in it could deserve endless suffering. A punishment should be proportionate to the offense.
licoes.a: More voices: Hume also pointed out that a punishment without purpose, when it can no longer correct or protect anyone, does not fit our idea of goodness. Constantine legalized Christianity in 313 and convened Nicaea in 325, where most bishops rejected Arius' thesis. He gave imperial power to the Church, and that changed a lot; but he didn't invent it.
licoes.a: Inside reading: What Constantine actually did is more important than the myth: the faith of the persecuted became the religion of the empire. That's where the blending of spirituality and power begins. Practice: always separate the message of a master from the use that power has made of it.

licoes.t: Fluoride calcifies the pineal gland to block awakening.
p: fluoride calcifies the pineal gland to block awakening
licoes.r: Myth in the form in which it usually circulates. Calcification of the pineal gland is common and increases with age, and a small study from 2001 found accumulated fluoride in it. But there is no evidence that this blocks any spiritual capacity, nor of a plan for it. Fluoride in water, in the doses used, reduces cavities, according to the WHO.
licoes.a: Inner reading: The third eye, in traditions, is a symbol of inner vision, which develops with attention and silence, not with a fluoride-free diet. Seeking awakening in an external enemy is another form of the Matrix. Practice: Ten minutes of silence with your eyes closed is worth more than any detox.

licoes.t: The Christians burned the Library of Alexandria
p: who burned the library of alexandria
fire of the library of alexandria
the christians burned the library of alexandria
quem queimou a biblioteca de alexandria
licoes.r: A simplification that became a myth. The Library of Alexandria did not disappear in a single fire: it declined over the centuries, with budget cuts, the expulsion of scholars in 145 B.C., and a fire in Julius Caesar's war in 48 B.C. In 391 C.E., Christians destroyed the Serapeum, a temple that housed part of a collection; it is not known how many books remained there.
licoes.a: Inside reading: the real story accuses several culprits and above all negligence, which kills knowledge slowly. A single villain is easier to hate, but less teachable. Practice: support a library, a teacher or an open knowledge project.

licoes.r: The vast majority of historians, believers and nonbelievers, accept that Jesus of Nazareth existed: a Jewish preacher from Galilee, baptized by John and crucified under Pontius Pilate. In addition to the Gospels and Paul, he is mentioned by the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus and by the Roman Tacitus. The thesis that he never existed is in the minority. Miracles and the resurrection are already a matter of faith, not history.
licoes.a: Inner reading: calculated truth separates what history holds, existence and crucifixion, from what is belief, miracles. That respects the believer and the skeptic at the same time. Practice: Read the Sermon on the Mount as the words of a real man, and see what they do for you.

licoes.r: Marguerite Porete was born around 1250, probably in the county of Hainaut, between France and the Holy Roman Empire. She was a highly educated woman and a beguine, one of the women who lived their faith freely, without convent vows and without a husband. She wrote The Mirror of Simple Souls and was burned alive in Paris on 1 June 1310.
licoes.a: Almost everything we know about her comes from the trial records, written by those who wanted to silence her. Even so, the portrait that remains is clear: a writer who dared to think about the sacred with her own mind and in the language of the people. No authentic portrait of her exists; the images in the memorial are artistic representations. Say Marguerite memorial to open the full page, with audio in Portuguese a

licoes.r: In the 1290s Marguerite wrote, in Old French, the language of the people, and not in Latin, The Mirror of Simple and Annihilated Souls. It is a dialogue between the Soul, Love and Reason. The Soul passes through seven states until it lets go of everything that is only its own and becomes transparent, like a mirror, to divine love.
licoes.a: She calls this annihilation: not the death of the person, but the end of the prison of the ego. Such a soul no longer lives out of fear of punishment or by trading favours with heaven; it lives free, because it loves. In chapter 22 she compares the free soul to the eagle, which flies higher than all other birds. For the power of that time, this freedom was the danger: whoever finds God through love no longer depends

licoes.r: Between 1296 and 1306 the bishop of Cambrai had the book burned in public in Valenciennes, in front of her. She did not obey the ban. Around 1308 she was arrested and handed over to the inquisitor of France, the Dominican William of Paris, the same man behind the trial of the Templars. She spent about a year and a half in prison and refused to take the oath or to answer.
licoes.a: Unable to question her, the inquisitors put the book on trial. They took fifteen sentences from it, the articles, and in April 1310 twenty-one theologians of the University of Paris declared them heretical. Today only three of the fifteen articles can be identified with certainty. Because she had kept spreading a book already condemned, she was declared a relapsed heretic. Earlier, three churchmen, among them Godfrey

p: a mulher que sorriu na fogueira
licoes.r: On 1 June 1310, at the Place de Grève in Paris, where the City Hall square is today, Marguerite Porete was burned alive. She did not recant. The continuation of the chronicle of Guillaume de Nangis, written by someone with no sympathy for her, recorded that she faced death so calmly that the crowd wept.
licoes.a: About the phrase the woman who smiled at the stake: the sources speak of calm and serenity, and say the people wept; no source of the time says she smiled. The smile is a poetic reading of that peace. The beguin Guiard de Cressonessart, who tried to defend her, confessed under pressure and was sentenced to life in prison. They burned the woman; they could not burn what she had understood.

licoes.t: After the fire: the nameless book
p: after the fire the nameless book
licoes.r: The book survived without her name. It was copied and translated into Latin, Italian and Middle English, and travelled through several countries, read by monks and nuns who did not know they were reading a condemned woman. Only in 1946 did the Italian historian Romana Guarnieri recognise Marguerite Porete's book in Latin manuscripts of the Vatican Library.
licoes.a: Before that, the Mirror was even attributed to other authors, and in 1927 it was printed in English as the work of an unknown French mystic, in Clare Kirchberger's edition. Six hundred and thirty-six years after the fire, she got her own name back.

licoes.t: Victims of the Inquisition: the memorial
p: victims of the inquisition the memorial
how many did the inquisition kill
licoes.r: Marguerite was not the only one. Historians estimate that the Spanish Inquisition prosecuted about one hundred and fifty thousand people and sent between three thousand and five thousand to their deaths. The Portuguese Inquisition, which also reached Brazil, burned at least one thousand one hundred and seventy-five people alive, according to Henry Charles Lea.
licoes.a: Among the victims of the Portuguese Inquisition was the Rio-born playwright Antônio José da Silva, executed in Lisbon in 1739. In Europe's witch hunts, driven by church courts and also by secular courts, Catholic and Protestant alike, between forty thousand and sixty thousand people were executed, most of them women. Historians themselves warn that these numbers are minimums: many deaths in prison and under torture w

licoes.r: The memorial has a text written as a tribute, as if she were speaking. Note: it is an imagined text, not a historical speech. It begins: I am Marguerite. I have no portrait; nobody painted my face. They kept only the accusations against me. But I left a mirror.
licoes.a: And it ends: My name is Marguerite, and through my name speak thousands who could not finish their sentence. Finish it for us. Think freely. Love without fear. Her real words are in the book. In chapter 6 the Soul says: Virtues, I take leave of you for evermore; now shall mine heart be more free and more in peace. And in chapter 22 the free soul is compared to the eagle, which flies higher than any other bird.

licoes.r: The original book can be downloaded for free, in public-domain editions only: the fifteenth-century Chantilly manuscript, as a two-hundred-and-fifty-six-page PDF on Wikimedia Commons; the full Middle French text transcribed by Wikisource; and the medieval English translation published in 1927, on the Internet Archive.
licoes.a: The links are in the memorial, in the section The book, and in the sources of this lesson. The Wikisource transcription is CC BY-SA 4.0 and is stored in the app to read offline. Modern translations are under copyright, so they are listed only as references, without files.

licoes.r: Marguerite's story asks each of us: who has the right to decide what you may think, read, write and feel about the sacred? For centuries, institutions that claimed to speak in God's name used fear, fire and silence to control consciences.
licoes.a: What is denounced here is not sincere faith, but dogma armed with power, the idea that truth needs jailers. Freedom of conscience, of thought and of knowledge was won with lives like hers. Every time someone thinks for themselves, asks without fear and shares what they learned, Marguerite's flame stays lit, not as a fire, but as light.

Situação Taxa (GRU) Passaporte comum (primeira vez ou renovação) R$ 257,25 Urgência/emergência (comprovada) R$ 334,42 (R$ 257,25 + R$ 77,17) Passaporte anterior válido perdido/extraviado R$ 514,50 Preencha o formulário online no site oficial da Polícia Federal (gov.br/pf → Passaporte → Solicitar). Tenha em mãos RG/CNH, CPF, título de eleitor e endereço com CEP. Pague a GRU (gerada no fim do formulário): PIX ou cartão pelo PagTesouro (compensa em minutos) ou boleto (até 72h). Não pague o boleto por transferência comum.

Agende o atendimento no mesmo sistema depois que o pagamento compensar. Escolha um posto perto: o passaporte é retirado no mesmo lugar. Vá ao atendimento com os originais: documento de identidade com naturalidade (RG, CNH com naturalidade ou equivalente), CPF, comprovante de quitação eleitoral (se obrigado a votar), certificado de reservista (homens de 19 a 45 anos), passaporte anterior (se tiver) e o protocolo. Ali tiram foto e digitais. Retire o passaporte : em geral fica pronto em cerca de 6 dias úteis (pode chegar a ~10 em alguns postos).
